articles.title: How I built a private, animated web home for two (and run it for $4/month)
articles.description: Most apps for couples feel like either a chat client with streaks bolted on, or a $10/month...
articles.body_html:
Most apps for couples feel like either a chat client with streaks bolted on, or a $10/month subscription wall. I originally built quzora as a private, animated home for my own relationship: a wooden railway timeline of memories, ruled notebook pages you write on directly, a fairy-lit polaroid photo wall, wax-sealed letters, an 82-word feelings wheel, a shared list, and celebration reminders.

Once it grew into a real multi-tenant app, I wanted to keep the architecture simple enough for one person to maintain and cheap enough to stay free. Here are four technical choices that paid off the most.

1. One container, zero idle-wake pain, $4/month

Instead of splitting frontend, API, workers, and a media proxy across five services, everything ships as one multi-stage Docker container on Fly.io (React 19 + Vite + Tailwind v4 on the client, Express 4 + Drizzle ORM on the server, Neon Postgres for data, Cloudflare R2 for media).

Two small details made it feel fast without costing much:

  • One always-on machine (min_machines_running = 1): Auto-stopping saved a couple dollars a month, but a 2-second cold boot feels awful when someone opens the app just to read a letter.
  • A database-free /healthz probe: Fly polls /healthz every 30 seconds. Because that route deliberately never touches Postgres, Neon still scales to zero overnight while the Express process stays warm.

Total monthly cost at couple scale: ~$4 for Fly, $0 on Neon, $0 on R2 (zero egress), $0 on WorkOS AuthKit, $0 on Resend.

2. Lazy WebP variants and locked-down /media/*

Photos and videos are 99% of the bytes in a memory app, and an unguessable S3 URL is not real privacy. Every media request goes through GET /media/<key> on Express, which enforces both authentication and couple ownership before streaming a byte.

To keep the photo wall snappy on phones:

  • Originals are stored untouched in R2 as masters.
  • Feed thumbnails (?w=800) and lightbox views (?w=1600) are generated lazily on first request with sharp (EXIF-rotated, resize-first, WebP quality 80) and cached beside the original with Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable. A 5 MB phone photo drops to ~90 KB.
  • Videos never download in the feed. ffmpeg extracts a single poster frame lazily (?poster), and tapping play streams the original via HTTP range requests.

3. Importing from Google Photos (and the COOP popup gotcha)

Google deprecated full library access in favor of the Google Photos Picker API, which is actually better for privacy because the app only ever sees the exact photos the user selects.

The sneaky bug: Google's picker sends Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, which severs the popup from window.opener. That means postMessage fails and popup.closed reads true while the picker is still wide open.

The fix was treating the popup as fire-and-forget and having the main app tab poll a lightweight status endpoint (connecting -> picking -> ready). Once ready, the server streams the import back as NDJSON so each polaroid lands on the photo wall the moment its WebP variant is ready, carrying its original createTime date.

4. Prerendered public pages + Markdown twins without Next.js

Because the signed-in app is a heavy client-side SPA, I didn't want to rewrite everything in a meta-framework just for SEO. Instead, npm run build runs a 60ms Vite SSR pass (renderToString) over the public landing page, guides, and a set of free zero-login couples tools (a days-together calculator, an interactive feelings wheel, an open-when prompt picker, and a bucket list generator).

During that same build step, a small script converts each prerendered HTML page into a clean .md twin (stripping SVGs, nav chrome, and decorative mockups). Express serves the Markdown version whenever an AI agent or curl asks for .md or sends Accept: text/markdown, alongside llms.txt and JSON-LD schemas.

If you'd like to try the app, it's free to use. Check it out at quzora.com.

Hey DEV Community!

I'm Apoorv Karanwal, a student, developer, and technology enthusiast. Today, I want to share something I've been working on — building my own social media platform, KW EduNet, from scratch.

💡 The Idea

It started with a simple thought:

What if students had their own digital platform where they could connect, learn, share knowledge, and interact with AI — all in one place?

I didn't want to build just another social media application. I wanted to create something that could make students' everyday digital experience more useful.

That's how KW EduNet started.

🛠️ Building Everything from Scratch

Building a platform is very different from just having an idea.

I had to think about the complete experience — from the user interface to the functionality behind every feature.

Some of the things I've been working on include:

  • User Profiles: Personalized student profiles.
  • Social Feed: A space where students can share posts and ideas.
  • AI Integration: An AI-powered experience for asking questions and learning.
  • Communities: Spaces for students to connect around shared interests.
  • Study Features: Tools such as flashcards, bookmarks, and learning resources.
  • Messaging: A way for students to communicate.
  • Gamification: Leaderboards and interactive experiences to make learning more engaging.

The goal is to make these features work together as one connected platform.

⚙️ Technology Behind the Project

For the development, I've been working with:

  • React
  • Vite
  • TypeScript
  • Firebase
  • AI integration

I wanted to build a modern, responsive application with a strong foundation that could grow as the platform evolves.

🧠 What I've Learned

This project has taught me that building software isn't just about writing code.

It's also about:

  • Understanding real user problems.
  • Designing meaningful user experiences.
  • Thinking about application architecture.
  • Handling authentication and data.
  • Considering security and privacy.
  • Finding and fixing bugs.
  • Improving the product through continuous iteration.

One important lesson I've learned is that a feature isn't truly complete just because it looks good. It needs to work reliably too.

🚀 What's Next?

KW EduNet is currently in its beta development journey.

There is still a lot to improve, test, and build. My next focus is making the platform more reliable, improving the user experience, and bringing its first real student community onboard.

I'm not claiming to have built the next big social network. I'm simply sharing what I'm learning while trying to build something meaningful.

A Small Introduction

I'm Apoorv Karanwal, a student interested in software development, artificial intelligence, robotics, and entrepreneurship.

Building KW EduNet has been one of my most interesting learning experiences so far.

This is just the beginning.

I'd love to hear from other developers:

Have you ever built a complete application from scratch? What was the most challenging part of your journey?

Let's connect and learn together!

Developer: Apoorv Karanwal

articles.body_html:
A Little Chinese Philosophy Over Coffee

An Ordinary Afternoon

The afternoon was quiet.

Sunlight came through the front window of the café, falling across the table by the window. It was the best seat in the place, though I had never officially declared it so. Regulars seemed to discover that on their own.

I was wiping down the counter when the bell above the door rang.

A familiar customer walked in, a laptop bag over his shoulder and the unmistakable expression of someone who had spent the entire day in meetings.

“The usual?”

“Please. Something a little stronger today.”

“Rough day?”

He took the seat by the window.

“You have no idea. Product wants everything done yesterday. Development says the requirements keep changing. QA keeps finding problems. Infrastructure says nobody understands how much work deployment actually takes. And the business team just wants to know why we haven't launched yet.”

I started grinding the coffee beans.

“Sounds like a perfectly healthy company.”

He looked up at me.

“Are you joking?”

“Just a little.”

I poured the coffee and placed the cup in front of him.

“Actually, there's an ancient Chinese idea that might help explain what you just described.”

He took a sip.

“Please don't tell me it's another management framework.”

“Not a framework. No slides, either. Just an old way of looking at how things relate to one another.”

I leaned against the counter.

“It's called the Five Elements.”

Five Elements, Not Five Departments

He looked at me with mild suspicion.

“The Five Elements?”

“Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water.”

I counted them off on my fingers.

“In Chinese, we call it Wu Xing. It's an ancient way of understanding relationships and changes in the world. It isn't simply about putting five things next to each other. The interesting part is how they interact.”

He glanced around the café.

“So where have you hidden them? Behind the coffee machine?”

I laughed.

“You can see them right now. Wooden tables, metal equipment, water in your cup, heat from the coffee machine, and the ground beneath this building. You just haven't started charging rent for them.”

He laughed and took another sip.

“Fine. So how does this explain my company?”

“Let's try something. Imagine your IT company has five elements of its own.”

A Little Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water

I picked up a clean cup and slowly turned it in my hand.

“Let's start with Wood.”

Wood grows. It reaches outward, puts out branches, and looks for more room.

“In an IT company, I'd associate Wood with the Product team. Product people decide what the company should build, what users might need, and which direction the product should grow.”

“So Product is the tree?”

“More or less. Though some product roadmaps look more like forests nobody has bothered to trim.”

He laughed.

“That sounds familiar.”

I put the cup back on the counter.

“Next comes Fire.”

Fire brings energy. It spreads, attracts attention, and makes things stand out.

“I'd associate Fire with Business Operations: the business and growth side of the company. They take the value created by the product and bring it to users. They help people discover it, use it, and, ideally, generate revenue.”

“Ideally?”

“Well, running a café has taught me one thing: never calculate tomorrow's revenue before the customers have even walked through the door.”

He laughed.

“Fair enough.”

I picked up the milk pitcher, rinsed it, and turned it upside down on the towel.

“Next is Earth. Earth supports everything. It gives other things somewhere to stand.”

“In an IT company, I'd associate Earth with Infrastructure Operations. Servers, networks, databases, deployment environments, monitoring systems, and everything else that keeps the systems running.”

“So, the people nobody notices until something breaks?”

“Exactly. When everything works, nobody asks how the ground beneath their feet is doing. The moment it disappears, suddenly everyone becomes an infrastructure expert.”

He nearly spilled his coffee laughing.

“That's painfully accurate.”

I picked up the coffee pot.

“Next is Metal. I'd associate Metal with Development.”

“Because developers like hardware?”

“Not quite. Think of Metal as something solid and precise, something that can be shaped into a tool. Developers turn ideas into working systems. They solve technical problems, build structures, and make things actually happen.”

“That's a pretty flattering description of us.”

“Don't get too comfortable. Every element has its problems.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“And Water?”

I glanced at the coffee cup in his hand.

“Water is Testing.”

He looked at me.

“Testing? Why Water?”

“Water flows. It passes through different places, finds gaps, reaches corners, and reveals the shape of the places it touches.”

I paused to refill the coffee pot.

“Testing should do something similar. It shouldn't just execute a checklist and report bugs. It should also help information flow between Product, Development, Business, and Infrastructure. It exposes risks, finds weak spots, and helps everyone see what's actually happening.”

“So QA is the water flowing through the whole company?”

“At least, that's how I see it.”

I put the coffee pot back on the warmer.

“Five elements, five different roles. But they're not five isolated departments.”

They Nourish One Another

He looked down at the notes he'd just typed into his phone.

“Okay. What comes next?”

“Now it gets interesting. In the Five Elements, there's a relationship called generating. Put simply, one element nourishes or supports another.”

I took a napkin and drew five small circles on it.

Wood generates Fire. Fire generates Earth. Earth generates Metal. Metal generates Water. Water generates Wood.


He stared at the napkin.

“That sounds like a rather strange company structure.”

“Give it a moment.”

I pointed to the first circle.

“Product creates value. Business Operations brings that value to the market. When the company makes money, it can invest some of that revenue in infrastructure.”

I moved to the next circle.

“Infrastructure supports Development. Development builds the system. Testing examines it, finds problems, and sends information back to Product.”

“And then Product keeps improving?”

“Exactly. And the cycle starts again.”

He studied the circles in silence for a few seconds.

“So nobody can really work completely independently.”

“At least, not for very long.”

I folded the napkin and slid it across the table.

A company keeps moving because work doesn't stop at the boundaries between departments.

Sometimes, Holding Each Other Back Is Necessary

He finished his coffee and leaned back in his chair.

“But if everyone is supposed to support everyone else, why do companies still argue so much?”

“Because there's another kind of relationship.”

I collected his empty cup and carried it to the sink.

“In Chinese, we call it overcoming. One element places limits on another.”

I rinsed the cup and put it back on the shelf.

“Think about your company. Product can't keep adding features forever. Development can't spend six months pursuing technical perfection for every little feature. Testing can't hold every release indefinitely. Business can't chase growth while ignoring quality. And Infrastructure can't reject every change just because things are stable right now.”

He nodded slowly.

“So sometimes they have to disagree.”

“Of course. A little disagreement can actually make a company healthier.”

I dried my hands.

Overcoming isn't about destroying the other side. It's about preventing one force from growing so much that the whole system can no longer handle it.

He glanced at the napkin again.

“That might be more useful than another team-building workshop.”

“Possibly. And it's cheaper. All you need is a napkin and a cup of coffee.”

There's More to the Story

The sunlight had shifted from one side of the table to the other. His coffee was gone, and he had finally stopped checking his phone every few minutes.

“Is that all there is to the Five Elements?”

I smiled and continued wiping the counter.

“Not even close.”

“I knew it.”

“There's much more to it. The relationships are far more complicated than five names and a circle. Each element has its own characteristics, too. Some things aren't quite as simple as they first appear.”

I glanced toward the window.

“Take Earth, for example. It's a little different from the other four.”

“How so?”

I picked up his empty cup.

That's a story for another cup.

He laughed.

“I'll remember that.”

“Good. I'm running a café. I need regular customers.”

He packed up his laptop and stood.

At the door, he turned around.

“So, which element do you think I am? Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, or Water?”

I pretended to think carefully.

“Today? Probably Water. You've spent the whole week flowing from one meeting to another.”

He shook his head, laughing.

“See you next time.”

“Your seat will be waiting.”

The door closed behind him.

I looked at the napkin he'd left on the table. Five little circles, with a few lines connecting them.

I picked it up, folded it, and placed it beside the coffee machine.

There were plenty of other things we could talk about.

Just not today.

The afternoon was still warm, the coffee was still good, and another customer was already walking toward the door.

P.S. English isn't my first language, so I use AI to help polish my writing and smooth out the rough edges. Thanks for reading.

☕ Buy me a coffee

P.P.S. The paperback edition of my earlier book is now available.

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

DRY STATIC is a dry breath-hold trainer for freedivers that checks each hold with the camera instead of trusting a stopwatch.

Freedivers train on land every day with CO2 and O2 tables: a set of timed holds and rests, done seated or lying down, never in water. Today's table apps are timers. You tap to say the hold started, you tap for your first contraction, you tap when it ends. Nothing checks whether the hold was real, whether you sneaked a breath, or when the involuntary diaphragm contractions began.

DRY STATIC runs the same tables, but it watches the breathing waveform from the SmartSpectra SDK while each hold runs:

  • A hold is verified, not assumed. During a real hold the chest and abdomen traces go flat. Each hold ends as verified, breath detected, or partly readable, with the share of the hold the camera could actually see.
  • Contraction marks (experimental). Diaphragm contractions show up as short jerks in the abdominal trace. The app marks them and scores the marks against your own taps.
  • Pulse only after the hold. The SDK's pulse is a 12-second average, so showing it mid-hold would misstate when it was measured. It appears in the round summary, with the drop across the hold.

There is no dashboard, no streaks and no score. Each round gets a strip chart and at most three plain sentences.

Demo

The video plays the bundled replay (a synthetic recording, labeled as such in the app) at 4x speed, then shows the analyzer output from a real session of three dry holds.

Code

chintandb / dry-static

DRY STATIC

A dry apnea table trainer for freedivers that uses the camera to check each hold.

Freedivers train breath-holds on land with CO2 and O2 tables: a fixed series of timed holds and rests, done seated or lying down. Most table apps are a stopwatch, and nothing checks the hold itself. A small breath, a pause to talk, or a lost camera view all pass unnoticed. DRY STATIC reads the breathing traces from the Presage SmartSpectra SDK and uses them for three things: it checks that each hold stayed still, it marks diaphragm contractions (experimental), and it shows how your pulse changed after each hold.

It is a desktop app built with Electron and TypeScript. It runs on macOS with Apple Silicon and needs Node.js 20 or newer.

Demo video (2:54): docs/demo.mp4. It plays the bundled synthetic recording at 4x speed, then shows the analyzer output from a…

View on GitHub

Try it with no key and no camera:

git clone https://github.com/chintandb/dry-static.git
cd dry-static
npm install
npm run replay   # bundled synthetic recording
npm test         # 186 tests, no camera or key

Live mode: cp .env.example .env, add your PRESAGE_API_KEY, then npm start. macOS arm64.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Signals used: chest breathing trace, abdominal breathing trace, breathing rate, pulse rate, and the talking flag. If the key refuses that set, the app falls back to the three breathing metrics alone. It also listens to the SDK's validation codes and hints.

What happens in real time:

  1. Framing. The SDK's validation hints ("move back", "chest not visible" and so on) are turned into one short instruction. Continue unlocks only after the SDK reports a good view for 3 s and both breathing traces are arriving.
  2. Settle-in, 45 s. The app learns how big your normal breathing is on each trace, picks the cleaner one, and records your resting pulse.
  3. During each hold a status chip updates live:
    • HOLD VERIFIED while the trace stays flat.
    • BREATH DETECTED if the trace moves away from its recent baseline by more than 0.4x your normal breathing size for at least 0.4 s. The baseline is a trailing 12 s median, so a quick exhale-and-sip shows up instead of being averaged away.
    • NOT READABLE when samples stop for more than 1.5 s, the SDK's validation code stays bad for more than 1.5 s, or the SDK reports talking. A hold is never smoothed over.
  4. After each hold: the verdict, your pulse curve and drop, and your breathing rate as it recovers.

Integration. It is an Electron app. The renderer runs the SmartSpectra Node SDK on the camera stream, and the main process holds the API key and the SDK's IPC bridge, so the key never reaches the page. The renderer is sandboxed. Every packet is timestamped on the SDK clock, and taps are mapped onto that clock through a median offset, so marks and taps line up. Telemetry is off. The same detectors run offline over recorded sessions (npm run analyze), which is how they were tested.

What a real session showed. I recorded three real dry holds (27 s, 13 s, 27 s):

Result
Hold verdicts 3 of 3 verified, 98–99.5% of each hold readable, 30 Hz, no gap over 0.03 s
Pulse drop −7.7 and −17.3 BPM (round 1 had no pulse reading before the hold)
Contraction marks vs my taps 0 of 6 matched. My waist was out of frame, so there was no abdominal trace

The first version flagged all three real holds as breaths. Two things from the real data changed the detector:

  • The chest kept settling for 5 to 8 s after the last inhale, so the first 8 s of a hold are now ignored (it was 3 s).
  • A felt contraction moved the chest trace 0.74x my normal breathing size for 1.6 s, which is enough to look like a breath. A short movement (2.5 s or less) next to a contraction tap is now excused, and the round summary lists it instead of hiding it.

The pass/fail thresholds were written before any data. Contraction marks failed them, so they stay labeled experimental.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use.

The need. In apnea training, how long a hold lasted and when contractions started are the main progress markers, and today they are self-reported. A camera that can see a breath makes the training log honest without a chest strap or any extra hardware.

Who it's for. Freedivers and breath-hold trainees doing dry tables at home, seated, with a laptop.

Designed for them:

  • Safety before the camera. Six checks (dry land, seated or lying down, someone nearby, no hyperventilation, stop at the first strong urge) must all be ticked before the camera opens. Holds are capped at 50–60% of your personal best, below the usual top of a classic O2 table, and nothing ever extends a hold. Stop is always one click away.
  • Honest output. Every verdict says how much of the hold was readable. A short movement excused by a contraction tap is still listed. Pulse is never shown during a hold because it lags.
  • Calm interface. One chip, one trace, a big timer. No rankings and no streaks that would push someone to hold longer.
  • Works without a key. Replay mode and the offline analyzer let anyone check the detectors without a camera or a trial.

Consent and Data Handling

Consent. The first screen says what the app does, what the camera is used for, what is stored, and that telemetry is off, before anything opens. The safety screen follows. The camera opens only after both, and only for the length of a session. The app grants camera access (video only, no microphone) to its own bundled page and denies every other permission request.

What is stored. Only numbers: breathing trace values, breathing rate, pulse rate, the talking flag, the SDK's validation codes, and the app's own timings (hold start and end, taps). No video, no images, no face data, and no text are stored.

Where. Everything stays on the Mac, in the app's data folder (~/Library/Application Support/dry-static/data; the About & Data screen shows the exact path): session summaries, recordings of the signal values, and a local count of live minutes used.

Sharing. Nothing is shared. The SmartSpectra SDK processes the camera feed and contacts Presage for authentication and processing; that is the SDK's own traffic. SDK telemetry is switched off (enableTelemetry: false), the app requests no Presage cloud insights, and it uses no AI service and makes no other network requests. There is no account, no analytics and no tracker.

Retention and deletion. Data stays until you delete it. One "Delete all data" button, on History and on About & Data, removes the whole data folder. CSV and PNG exports are written only to a file you choose.

The key. PRESAGE_API_KEY is read from .env or the environment in the main process. It is never logged, never shown, and never written into a recording. .env is git-ignored.

Not a medical device. DRY STATIC is a training aid for dry breath-hold practice. It does not measure oxygen or carbon dioxide, it cannot detect a blackout, and it is not a safety device. Never use it in or near water. People with heart, lung, blood-pressure or seizure conditions, and anyone pregnant, should talk to a doctor before starting breath-hold training. SmartSpectra metrics are for general wellness and informational purposes only and have not been cleared by the FDA.

articles.title: Coding agents won't replace you, but they're changing what "senior" means
articles.description: "Will AI replace developers?" is the wrong question. The better one is: which of your skills just got...
articles.body_html:
"Will AI replace developers?" is the wrong question. The better one is: which of your skills just got cheaper, and which got a lot more expensive?

The wrong debate

Cognition, the company behind the Devin coding agent, is reportedly weighing a funding round at a $70–80bn valuation, up from the $48bn it was valued at in its previous round. Investors are betting very large sums that agents will write a big share of the world's code.

They may well be right. But "agents write the code" and "developers disappear" are two very different claims. What's actually happening is quieter and more interesting: the job is shifting from producing code to directing, checking and owning it. That shift is redefining what it means to be senior.

What agents are now genuinely good at

Be honest about this part, because pretending agents are bad at coding is not a career strategy. Today's coding agents can reliably:

  • Turn a clear spec into working code across several files
  • Write tests, boilerplate, migrations and glue code faster than any human
  • Read an unfamiliar codebase and explain it
  • Fix well-described bugs, often on the first attempt
  • Translate between languages, frameworks and API versions

In other words, the tasks that used to fill a junior or mid-level developer's week, and a good share of a senior's, are now the cheap part.

The new senior skills

When writing code gets cheap, everything around it gets more valuable. Here's how the senior skill set is shifting:

Used to signal "senior" Now signals "senior"
Writes code fast Writes specs an agent can't misread
Knows the framework's API by heart Knows which architecture will still make sense in two years
Reviews a teammate's PR Reviews 2,000 lines of agent output without rubber-stamping it
Debugs their own code Debugs systems nobody fully wrote by hand
Owns a feature Owns the outcome: correctness, security, cost, and the 3 a.m. pager

The common thread is judgment. An agent can produce ten plausible solutions. A senior engineer knows which one is right for this system, this team and this business, and can explain why.

There's also a new skill nobody had a name for two years ago: knowing when not to trust the output. Recent debates over AI-generated proofs that are formally verified but that no human fully understands are a preview of the same problem in code review.

So what happens to juniors?

This is the uncomfortable part. Juniors traditionally built judgment by writing a lot of mediocre code and getting it reviewed. If agents write that code, where does the judgment come from?

I don't think the answer is "stop hiring juniors". Teams that do that will have no seniors in five years. The answer is to change what junior work looks like:

  • Juniors review and test agent output, and must explain why it's right before it merges
  • They write the specs and acceptance criteria, not just the code
  • They debug production issues alongside seniors, where judgment is actually learned
  • Some tasks are done deliberately without an agent, the way pilots still practice flying manually

How to level up this year

Whatever your title, these habits put you on the right side of the shift:

  1. Write the spec before the prompt. Define inputs, outputs, edge cases and what "done" means. You'll get better agent output and build a skill that transfers everywhere.
  2. Read every diff like you'll be paged for it. Because you will be.
  3. Learn the layers agents are weakest at: system design, data modeling, security, performance and cost.
  4. Get good at evaluation. Build tests and checks that catch an agent's mistakes automatically.
  5. Own outcomes, not tickets. Talk to users, understand the business, and measure whether what shipped actually worked.
  6. Keep your fundamentals sharp. Occasionally solve something without an agent, so you can still tell when it's wrong.

The fair counterpoint

The strongest argument against this post goes like this: agents are improving fast enough that judgment, review and design will be automated too, and "move up the stack" is just a slower way of being replaced. Others point out that if each engineer gets several times more productive, companies may simply need fewer of them, even if the job doesn't vanish.

Both are reasonable. My bet is that responsibility is the last thing to be automated. Someone still has to own the decision, the outage and the consequences. For now that's a person, and the people who are good at it are the new seniors.

Where do you land? Has a coding agent changed what your team expects from senior engineers? Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: Local AI Code Review Before a PR: Tools That Catch Bugs Before You Push
articles.description: Hello Devs 👋  Here's a situation many developers will recognize.  You've finished implementing a...
articles.body_html:
Hello Devs 👋

Here's a situation many developers will recognize.

You've finished implementing a feature. The tests are passing, the code looks reasonable, and you're getting ready to open a pull request. Before doing that, you take another look at the diff and notice a missing null check, an incorrect condition, or an edge case you didn't consider while writing the code.

It happens. Sometimes you catch it yourself, and sometimes the PR reviewer catches it later.

Now imagine having an AI code reviewer check your changes before you even create the pull request.

That's the idea behind local AI code review.

Instead of waiting for a PR to be opened, you can ask a review tool to inspect your current Git changes, identify potential problems, and return findings while the code is still sitting on your machine.

I think this is becoming an important part of AI-assisted development, especially when developers are using coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

Let's look at the tools that support this workflow and what makes their approaches different.

Why review code before opening a PR?

The usual AI code review workflow looks something like this:

Developer writes code
        |
        v
Commit and push changes
        |
        v
Open pull request
        |
        v
AI code review
        |
        v
Fix reported issues
        |
        v
Request another review

There is nothing wrong with this workflow. PR reviews are important, and they provide a useful place for developers to discuss changes.

But there is one limitation. By the time the review happens, the developer has already finished the implementation and moved into the review process. If the tool finds a problem, the developer has to go back, understand the finding, make the correction, push another update, and wait for another review.

With local review, you can move that feedback earlier.

Developer writes code
        |
        v
Run tests
        |
        v
Review local changes
        |
        v
Fix findings
        |
        v
Run tests again
        |
        v
Open pull request

The advantage isn't that you no longer need PR reviews. It's that you can catch some problems before asking another developer to review your work.

For coding agents, this becomes even more useful. The agent can write the code, request an independent review, inspect the findings, and fix the issues while it still has the implementation context.

What should a local code review tool actually review?

This is something I would check before choosing a tool.

A local review tool should ideally understand more than the last commit.

For example, imagine you've modified three existing files, created two new files, and haven't committed anything yet. If the review tool only checks committed changes, it won't see the complete implementation.

A useful local review should be able to inspect:

  • Modified and staged files.
  • Uncommitted changes in the working tree.
  • New and untracked files.
  • The difference between your branch and its intended base branch.
  • The purpose of the change, including relevant tickets or specifications.
  • Related code and dependencies that might be affected.

The last two points are particularly important. A reviewer that only sees a diff may misunderstand why you made a particular change or flag something that was an intentional design decision.

Some tools can also provide structured findings that a coding agent can process directly. That makes it possible to build a review-and-fix loop without manually copying every finding into another prompt.

1. Qodo: Local review through the CLI and Agentic Toolbox

Qodo is particularly interesting here because local review is connected to its broader code review and coding-agent workflow.

With Qodo's Agentic Toolbox, developers can use the qodo-review skill to review local changes before opening a pull request. It uses the same review engine as Qodo's PR review, but the review happens while the changes are still in the developer's working tree.

You can also run the review directly from the command line using the Qodo CLI.

For example:

qodo review

You don't need to create a pull request first.

The review can include committed and uncommitted changes, along with new and untracked files. You can also provide additional context, such as what the feature is supposed to do, important implementation decisions, and links to the ticket or specification.

This is useful because a code reviewer should understand the intention behind a change, not just compare two versions of a file.

There is another detail worth mentioning: your local changes don't need to be pushed for the review. The comparison base must be available remotely, but your working-tree changes can remain local.

Qodo collects the relevant changes and sends them to its review engine. It returns structured findings without pushing your code, creating a PR, or posting comments to your Git provider.

How the Agentic Toolbox changes the workflow

The CLI is useful on its own, but the more interesting part is how Qodo connects local review with coding agents.

Suppose you're using Claude Code or Codex to implement a new API endpoint.

The agent finishes the implementation and runs the tests. Instead of immediately preparing a pull request, you can ask it to review its local changes using Qodo.

The workflow looks like this:

Developer gives a task
        |
        v
Claude Code / Codex
        |
        v
Agent implements the feature
        |
        v
Tests run
        |
        v
Qodo independent review
        |
        v
Findings returned to the agent
        |
        v
Agent fixes approved issues
        |
        v
Developer checks the result
        |
        v
Pull request

The important distinction is that Qodo provides an independent review. The coding agent writes the implementation, while Qodo's review engine examines the resulting changes.

The qodo-review skill makes this available inside the coding-agent session. The agent can receive structured findings and use them to investigate and fix problems without requiring the developer to move between multiple tools.

You can also use the qodo-codebase-wisdom skill to investigate repository relationships, pull request history, and cross-repository dependencies before or during implementation. This adds useful context when a local change could affect code outside the current repository.

Qodo 3.0 and the bigger picture

Qodo 3.0 takes this beyond reviewing an individual diff. Its Software Map helps teams understand relationships between repositories and services, while PR Triage helps organize related pull requests and understand the potential impact of larger changes.

That broader context is useful when reviewing local work too. A change might look correct in the current repository but affect a shared API, library, or downstream service.

Combined with the Agentic Toolbox, the idea is to give coding agents access to relevant system context and an independent review step before their changes reach a pull request.

I think this is a meaningful difference from simply adding a review command to a terminal. The review becomes part of the development workflow, rather than another task developers remember to perform at the end.

Qodo is worth considering when you want local review, independent findings inside your coding agent, and access to broader codebase context before creating a PR.

2. CodeRabbit: Review local changes from the CLI

CodeRabbit is another tool to look at if you want AI code review directly from your terminal.

Its CLI brings CodeRabbit's review capabilities into a local development workflow. This means developers can ask for feedback on their changes without relying exclusively on the review process that starts after opening a pull request.

The advantage is convenience. Developers who already use CodeRabbit for PR reviews can also evaluate its CLI workflow before pushing their changes.

For example, after implementing a feature, you can run a local review and inspect the findings before creating the PR.

One thing I would check during evaluation is exactly which Git changes the CLI includes. Local review requirements vary, particularly when a developer has staged changes, uncommitted modifications, and newly created files in the same working tree.

Also remember that running a CLI locally doesn't necessarily mean the AI model runs locally. You should check CodeRabbit's data-processing and model configuration if your organization has source-code privacy requirements.

CodeRabbit is worth evaluating if your team already uses its PR review workflow and wants to bring review feedback closer to the developer's terminal.

3. Greptile: CLI-based review before pushing

Greptile is also worth considering for developers who prefer running AI code review from the command line.

Its CLI provides a way to bring Greptile's code review capabilities into the local development process, rather than relying only on pull request-based feedback.

This is useful when you want to inspect a change before sharing it with the rest of the team.

Greptile's codebase understanding is another relevant aspect. A review can benefit from knowing how the changed code relates to the wider repository, rather than examining every line without context.

However, I would test the exact local workflow before choosing it. Check whether it includes the uncommitted and untracked files you care about, how it handles branch comparisons, and whether findings can be passed back into your coding agent.

As with other CLI-based review tools, don't assume that the CLI itself means the model or review engine runs on your machine. Check the actual deployment and data-flow requirements.

Greptile is worth evaluating if you want to bring its codebase-aware review capabilities into a pre-PR workflow.

4. Macroscope: Local AI review from the terminal

Macroscope is another option in this category.

Its CLI is designed to review changes from your local branch before you push them. It brings review feedback into the terminal, so developers can identify potential bugs earlier instead of waiting for a pull request review.

The idea is similar to the other CLI tools: inspect the local changes, return findings, and give the developer an opportunity to fix problems before sharing the branch.

Macroscope is worth including in a comparison because local review is its focus, rather than treating the CLI as just another way to interact with a PR review product.

As always, check the details that matter to your workflow: which files are included, how the tool handles uncommitted changes, how it communicates findings, and whether it supports the coding agent you use.

Quick comparison

Here's how I would think about these options:

Tool Local review approach What stands out
Qodo CLI, Agentic Toolbox, MCP, coding-agent integrations Independent local review with session context and broader codebase understanding
CodeRabbit CLI Brings CodeRabbit review into the terminal workflow
Greptile CLI Codebase-aware review available in a local workflow
Macroscope CLI Focuses on reviewing local branch changes before pushing

One important point: a CLI review and a local model are two different things. A tool can inspect your local Git changes while sending the review request to a hosted service. If your requirement is that all analysis must happen on your machine, check model hosting and deployment separately.

What I would test before choosing one

I wouldn't choose a local review tool based only on the number of findings it reports.

I'd take a real feature branch and create a few different types of changes.

First, modify an existing function and leave the changes uncommitted. Then add a new file without staging it. Finally, make a change that depends on an existing API contract or business rule.

Run the review and check whether the tool understands the complete change.

I would pay particular attention to these questions:

  1. Does it review staged, unstaged, and untracked files?
  2. Can it compare the branch against the correct base?
  3. Can I provide the task description or design specification?
  4. Does it identify actual bugs, or mostly style and formatting issues?
  5. Are findings specific enough for a developer or coding agent to fix?
  6. Can it run inside Claude Code, Codex, or another agent?
  7. Does it review the changes independently of the coding agent?
  8. Does it understand dependencies outside the immediate diff?

Also check whether the tool modifies files automatically. Personally, I prefer a workflow where the reviewer reports findings and the developer or coding agent decides which fixes are appropriate. That keeps the review step separate from the decision to change code.

Does local review replace PR review?

No, and I don't think it should.

Local review is useful because it catches issues while the developer is still working on the change. But the final pull request can contain additional commits, merge conflicts, or changes introduced after the local review.

The PR also gives the rest of the team an opportunity to discuss the implementation, question architectural decisions, and check whether the change meets the original requirement.

I would use both stages:

Local review
    |
    | Catch issues during development
    v
Pull request review
    |
    | Validate the final shared change
    v
CI checks and human approval
    |
    v
Merge

Think of local review as an additional quality checkpoint, not a replacement for the team's existing review process.

Final Thoughts

I think local AI code review is one of the more practical additions to an AI-assisted development workflow.

When a coding agent can write a feature, run tests, and request an independent review before opening a PR, developers get feedback at a much more useful point in the process. They can fix problems while the implementation is still fresh instead of waiting for someone else to find them.

Qodo's Agentic Toolbox is particularly interesting because it connects local review with the coding agent itself. Its qodo-review skill can inspect local committed and uncommitted changes, include new files and coding-session context, and return structured findings before a PR exists. Qodo 3.0 adds a broader system context through Software Map and PR Triage, making it relevant for teams working across larger codebases.

CodeRabbit, Greptile, and Macroscope are also worth testing if you want terminal-based review options. The right choice depends on how much context you need, which coding agent you use, and how the tool handles your actual Git workflow.

For me, the ideal workflow is simple: let the coding agent implement the change, let an independent reviewer inspect it, fix the important findings, and only then open the pull request.

The earlier you find a problem, the less expensive it usually is to fix.

👨‍💻 TL;DR

If you want to review code before a pull request exists:

  • Qodo: Local CLI review and Agentic Toolbox integration, including committed, uncommitted, and untracked changes. Strong option when you want independent review inside your coding-agent workflow.
  • CodeRabbit: CLI-based local review, useful for teams already using CodeRabbit for PR reviews.
  • Greptile: CLI-based review with codebase understanding.
  • Macroscope: Terminal-focused review of local branch changes.

articles.title: BadUSB Works Because Trust Was Designed for Convenience, Not Verification
articles.description: Your computer does not ask if the keyboard is lying. It just starts typing.   Plug something...
articles.body_html:
Your computer does not ask if the keyboard is lying. It just starts typing.

Plug something into a USB port and watch what happens. Nothing asks for permission. Nothing asks for proof. The operating system sees a new device, reads a little ID card it hands over, and says, cool, welcome aboard. If that ID card says keyboard, the computer believes it. If it says mouse, it believes that too. If it says storage drive, network adapter, serial port, audio interface, or all five at once, it believes all of it.

That is not a bug that slipped through QA. That is the design. USB was built to make hardware disappear into the background, to make setup feel like magic. You plug it in, it works. No driver hunt, no config file, no interrogation. Convenience was the product. Verification was never invited to the meeting.

BadUSB lives in that gap.

It is not really about a specific stick, a specific brand, or a specific payload. It is about a protocol that trusts first and asks questions never. A BadUSB device is just a microcontroller that has learned to lie fluently in the language of USB descriptors. It tells your machine a story, and your machine, polite to a fault, believes every word.

This is why the attack feels almost unfair. It does not need you to click a sketchy link. It does not need you to disable your antivirus. It does not need a zero day. It just needs three seconds of physical access and a port that is feeling generous, which is to say, any port.

The lie starts before the operating system wakes up

When a USB device connects, it goes through enumeration. Think of it as a very short job interview where the applicant writes their own resume and the interviewer never calls references.

The device presents a vendor ID, a product ID, a device class, and a set of descriptors that say what it claims to be. The host reads them and loads the appropriate driver. A keyboard gets the HID driver. A flash drive gets the mass storage driver. A network adapter gets a network driver.

Here is the part that should make you uncomfortable: those IDs are not verified against a hardware root of trust. They are just numbers the firmware reports. A ten dollar microcontroller can claim to be a keyboard made by a major manufacturer, and Windows, macOS, and Linux will all nod along. There is no cryptographic signature on the claim. There is no challenge. There is no, prove you are who you say you are.

That is the first failure, and it is architectural. We built a universal bus for the entire planet and gave it the security model of a name tag at a conference. Hi, my name is KEYBOARD. Oh, great, come right in.

Once enumeration succeeds, the device is trusted. And trusted, in USB land, means powerful.

A keyboard is a god

People underestimate keyboards because they are boring. They sit there. They clack. They spill coffee. But from the perspective of an operating system, a keyboard is not a peripheral. A keyboard is a user.

When a keyboard sends keystrokes, the OS does not treat them as suggestions from an external gadget. It treats them as intent from the human sitting in front of the screen. That distinction matters enormously. A program trying to open a terminal, download a file, and run it would trigger a dozen alarms. A keyboard doing the exact same thing by typing the exact same commands is just... a person working.

BadUSB exploits that semantic loophole beautifully. It does not inject code through a vulnerability. It injects keystrokes through a trusted channel. It opens Run with Win plus R, types powershell, hits enter, types a one liner that pulls down a second stage, and hits enter again. To the machine, you just did that. To the logs, you just did that. To the security software watching for malicious processes, a human just did that, and humans are allowed to do weird things.

Speed is the other weapon. A BadUSB device can type at inhuman speed, hundreds of characters per second, with perfect accuracy, while also inserting delays exactly where a human would pause. It can wait for the desktop to load. It can wait for a UAC prompt and press the right arrow key. It can adapt. Modern payloads are not dumb scripts. They check the OS, check the keyboard layout, check if a window opened, and branch accordingly. They are tiny robots pretending to be you, and they are very good at it.

And because the attack happens at the HID layer, it bypasses almost everything we normally rely on. Antivirus does not scan keystrokes for malware. EDR does not flag a keyboard for typing too fast, at least not by default. Network firewalls do not care that the command to exfiltrate data was typed rather than downloaded. The whole defensive stack is built on the assumption that input from a keyboard equals input from a legitimate user. BadUSB breaks that assumption, then walks right through the hole.

It is not just keyboards anymore

The classic BadUSB story is the fake keyboard. The modern BadUSB story is much messier.

A single device can enumerate as multiple devices at once. It can be a keyboard and a mouse and a storage drive and a network adapter, all in one tiny package. That composite trick opens up attacks that look even more innocent.

Enumerate as a network adapter, for example, and you can hijack DNS. The computer thinks it just plugged in a new Ethernet dongle, assigns it a route, and starts sending traffic through it. Suddenly the attacker is in the middle, serving fake login pages, intercepting requests, downgrading connections. The user sees nothing. No popup. No warning. Just a slightly slower internet connection for a minute.

Enumerate as storage, and you can serve a fake installer. Enumerate as a serial device, and you can talk to internal tools that assume serial means local and safe. Enumerate as a mouse, and you can move the cursor, click through prompts, approve things the user never approved. The mouse does not need permission to click Allow. The mouse is allowed to click Allow. That is its job.

Even scarier, BadUSB devices can reprogram themselves on the fly. A drive that looks like boring storage when you first plug it in can flip to keyboard mode after a delay, or after it detects a specific OS, or after it receives a trigger. Firmware is software. Software can lie, wait, and change its story. The device you inspected five minutes ago is not necessarily the device you are plugged into now.

This is why the old advice, just do not plug in random USB drives, is both correct and completely insufficient. It assumes the threat is the drive you found in the parking lot. The real threat is any USB device whose firmware you do not control, which is to say, almost every USB device you own.

Why we cannot just patch this away

If BadUSB is so simple, why has it not been fixed in twenty years? Because fixing it would break the thing people actually love about USB: it just works.

Real verification would mean every USB device needs a cryptographic identity, every OS needs to check that identity against a trusted registry, and every user needs to approve new devices in a way that cannot be spoofed by a fake keyboard. That is doable in theory. It is miserable in practice.

Imagine plugging in a new mouse and getting a prompt that says, do you trust this mouse? Most people would click yes without reading. Then the fake keyboard would just type yes for them. Or it would wait until you approve a legitimate device, then piggyback on that approval. Human approval is a weak gate when the attacker controls an input device that can simulate human approval.

There are defenses, and they are worth using. USB device allowlisting, kernel level HID filtering, disabling USB ports in BIOS, using USB data blockers that only pass power, requiring physical presence for new devices, endpoint tools that alert on new HID devices appearing out of nowhere. All of them help. None of them are default. None of them are frictionless. And friction is exactly what USB was designed to eliminate.

Corporations can enforce strict policies. They can glue ports shut. They can deploy allowlists. They can train staff. Home users, small labs, makers, students, and everyone else living in the real world cannot realistically do that for every charger, every dongle, every borrowed cable, every conference swag stick.

So we live with the tradeoff. We chose convenience. We got convenience. We also got a universal attack surface shaped exactly like convenience.

The social engineering is the port itself

BadUSB is often framed as a hardware hack. It is better understood as a social hack that happens to use hardware.

The attack works because we have trained people, for decades, to trust ports. Plug in to charge. Plug in to present. Plug in to transfer photos. Plug in to use the printer. The port is a helpful hole in the side of the machine. It is not coded in our brains as a threat.

Attackers know this. That is why BadUSB payloads show up disguised as things people want to plug in: a free phone charger at an airport, a branded USB drive at a trade show, a replacement cable that looks identical to the real one, a promotional gadget that promises to speed up your computer. The device does not need to be found. It needs to be wanted.

Even without malice, the ecosystem is leaky. Cheap cables with hidden chips exist. Counterfeit devices with reprogrammable firmware exist. Supply chain tampering exists. You do not need a nation state actor to get a BadUSB device. You need an internet connection, a microcontroller, and a weekend. The barrier to entry is low, the payoff is high, and the victim often never knows what happened.

That asymmetry is the point. The defender has to secure every port, every device, every user, every time. The attacker has to get one device plugged in once.

What actually helps, if you are honest about it

Let us skip the fantasy advice. No one is going to stop using USB. No one is going to manually audit every descriptor of every device they own. So what moves the needle?

First, treat USB like network access, because that is what it is. A USB port is not a power outlet. It is a network interface that can pretend to be a user. If you would not plug an unknown Ethernet cable into your laptop, do not plug in an unknown USB device either. Same logic, same risk.

Second, separate charging from data. If you just need power, use a charge only cable or a USB data blocker. It is a dumb little adapter that cuts the data lines and only passes power. It turns a potentially hostile port into a dumb battery. Keep one in your bag. It is the cheapest security upgrade you will ever buy.

Third, assume any device that can type can own you. That means no borrowing keyboards at events, no plugging in that cool gadget your friend just built without checking it in a lab VM first, no using the free charging station that also wants to sync your phone. If a device enumerates as HID, it has the keys to the kingdom. Treat it accordingly.

Fourth, if you run a lab or a workspace, use allowlisting. It is annoying to set up, but it is the only defense that actually addresses enumeration. Only approved vendor and product IDs get to load drivers. Everything else gets blocked and logged. Pair that with alerts for new HID devices, and you at least get a signal when something weird shows up.

Fifth, practice the boring stuff. Lock your screen when you walk away. Disable autorun. Keep your OS patched, because BadUSB often chains into a second stage that does rely on a software bug. Use a separate, isolated machine or VM for testing unknown hardware. Never test a suspicious device on your main machine with your real accounts logged in. That is not paranoia. That is lab hygiene.

And finally, learn how the attack works by building it in a controlled lab, on your own hardware, with your own payloads, against machines you own. There is no better way to understand trust than to break it yourself, safely, and watch how easily a machine obeys a fake keyboard. Reading about BadUSB is interesting. Watching your own test laptop open a shell because a tiny board told it to is educational in a way no blog post can match.

Convenience was a choice, and we are still paying for it

BadUSB is not going away because the conditions that created it are not going away. We want devices that work instantly. We want ports that accept anything. We want zero friction. Vendors want to sell hardware that works everywhere. Operating systems want to be helpful. Users want to plug and play.

All of those wants are reasonable. All of them together create a system where identity is asserted, never proven, and where a keyboard is trusted absolutely because we never imagined a keyboard would lie.

The fix is not a single patch or a single product. It is a shift in mental model. Stop thinking of USB as a cable. Start thinking of it as a trust decision. Every time something goes into that port, you are making a decision about what you will allow to act as you, to see your network, to touch your files. That decision deserves a second of thought, even if the port was designed to make you skip it.

Your computer trusts too easily because we told it to. BadUSB just takes us at our word.

Further reading from numbpilled

If you want to go from understanding BadUSB to practicing it safely in your own lab, these guides go deep on authorized hardware testing, payload structure, and defensive setup:

Flipper Zero Black Book: 37 Flipper Zero techniques across BadUSB, NFC/RFID, Sub-GHz and BLE/Wi-Fi/GPIO

Flipper Zero Lab Manual: 37 Authorized Hardware Workflows

Vault Pass: 214-Product Numbpilled Archive Snapshot

AI Red Team Archive: LLM Security, Cloud Escalation and Defensive Testing

Hardware Lab Archive: RF, UART, Firmware and Cyberdeck Builds

All guides are for authorized use only: your own devices, data, and systems you have permission to test.
