articles.title: His Green Squares
articles.description: MONDAY: HIS   Kabir's profile is the first thing I see when I open my laptop on Monday...
articles.body_html:
MONDAY: HIS

Kabir's profile is the first thing I see when I open my laptop on Monday morning, because I left his tab open on Friday and never closed it. Forty-one weeks. A solid wall of green, no gaps, not one grey square in the whole row. The darkest green is the kind you get from twenty commits in a day. He has squares that dark in March, in July, in a week I know for a fact he was on holiday, because he sent me a photo of a beach and I replied with the thumbs-up emoji like a person who had never envied anyone in his life.

I scroll down to my own profile. My wall has a hole in it shaped like last Wednesday, when I spent the whole day reading a log file and changed nothing, and another hole shaped like the weekend, when I was not at my laptop at all. My green is the pale kind. Two commits, three commits, the colour of someone who showed up and did a normal amount of work.

Kabir walks past my desk with his coffee and asks what I'm working on. I tell him. He nods in the way people nod when they already knew the answer and asked anyway to be polite.

MONDAY: MINE

My Monday is a bug I cannot reproduce. It happens on the customer's machine and nowhere else. I spend four hours adding logging to a function I am fairly sure is innocent, and then I spend another hour staring at the logs it produces, which say the function is innocent. I commit nothing. There is nothing to commit. "Added logging, learned nothing" is not a commit message you push to a shared branch unless you want a conversation about it in standup.

At 6:40 I close the laptop. My square for today is grey. It will stay grey.

TUESDAY: HIS

Kabir commits at 09:12, 09:47, 10:03, 11:20, and 13:58. I know this because his graph updates while I am waiting for a build. Five commits before lunch. I have made one, and it is a comment I added to my own code because future me kept misunderstanding it, and I am not sure that counts as work even though it took twenty minutes to write the comment properly.

In the afternoon he pushes a fix with the message "typo". Then another one, also "typo". I open the second one. He changed "recieve" to "receive" in a readme. The commit is real. The diff is one word. The square is green either way.

TUESDAY: MINE

The bug reproduces. Once. At 11:04, on the customer's machine, while I am watching over a screen share, it happens exactly once and then never again. The customer laughs. I do not laugh. I write down the exact time, the exact click order, the exact version number, like a person taking notes at a crime scene where the criminal has already left.

I find it at 16:20. It is a race condition, two things finishing in the wrong order, and it only happens when the network is slow in one very specific way. The fix is eleven lines. I test it six times. It holds. I push at 17:02 with a message that says what the bug was and how the fix works, because the next person to read this code deserves to know. One commit. One pale green square. The best day of work I have had in a month, and the graph will never know the difference between this and the typo.

WEDNESDAY: HIS

Kabir is not at his desk. His status says "focus time" and his graph says he has already committed twice today, both before 9 a.m.

At lunch someone asks him how he stays so consistent. He shrugs and says he just commits every day. He says it the way people say they just run every morning, as if the sentence itself were the whole explanation. Nobody asks what the commits contain. I don't ask either. I am too busy deciding whether I am angry at him or at myself, and the answer is myself, and I hate that the answer is myself.

WEDNESDAY: MINE

I spend Wednesday in a design review for a feature that will not be built for three months. I say useful things. I draw a diagram on the whiteboard that three people photograph. I write no code. My square is grey by 3 p.m. and I know it will stay grey, and I catch myself thinking about whether I could push something small tonight, just to fill it, just so the week doesn't have a hole in it.

I could. I have a branch with a half-finished cleanup in it. I could push the half-finished cleanup. It would be green. It would also be a half-finished cleanup on the shared branch at 11 p.m., which is the kind of thing you do when the graph matters more than the code, and I sit there for a full minute with my hand on the laptop, deciding which one matters more to me.

I don't push it. I close the laptop and go home. The grey square stays grey.

THURSDAY: HIS

Kabir's wall hits forty-two weeks. Someone in the team chat posts a screenshot of it with a fire emoji. Three people react with the same emoji. Kabir replies with the folded-hands emoji, which is the correct reply, the humble reply, the reply of a man who did not ask for a screenshot of his graph to be posted in the team chat and also did not ask for it not to be.

I look at his graph again. Forty-two weeks, no gaps. I count the dark green squares. There are eleven of them. Eleven days with twenty or more commits. I think about what twenty commits in a day actually looks like, and the picture in my head is not a person doing twenty pieces of work. I don't know which one it is. I have never asked. Asking would sound like an accusation, and I am not sure it isn't one.

THURSDAY: MINE

The race-condition fix breaks something else. Of course it does. The thing it breaks is a report that nobody has looked at in six weeks, and it breaks it in a way that only shows up when the report is run on a Thursday, which is today. I find out at 10:15 from a message that starts "hey, quick question" and ends with a screenshot of numbers that are wrong in a way I recognise immediately, because I am the person who made them wrong yesterday.

I spend the day unbreaking it. The fix for the fix is four lines and a test that would have caught both bugs, the first one and the second one, if I had written it on Tuesday. I write it on Thursday instead. I push at 18:40. One commit. Pale green. The graph records a normal day.

FRIDAY: HIS

Kabir leaves early. He has a flight. His graph for today is already green, two commits before noon, and I know without checking that one of them says "typo" and the other one says "wip". Work in progress. A commit called "wip" is a square like any other. The wall does not ask what the work was.

FRIDAY: MINE

On Friday afternoon I deploy the race-condition fix for real. It goes out with the Thursday test and the four-line repair, and the customer's machine stops doing the thing it did once at 11:04 on Tuesday. The customer writes back, one line: "looks good, thanks". I read that line three times. It is the best code review I have had all week.

Then I do something I have not done in months. I open my own profile and look at my graph the way I have been looking at his. My wall has holes in it. Wednesday is grey. Last weekend is grey. The weekend before that is grey too. The green that is there is pale, two commits, three commits, one commit on Tuesday that mattered more than any five-commit day Kabir has had all month, and the graph cannot tell, and it will never be able to tell, because the graph was never measuring the work. It was measuring the pushing.

I scroll back up to Kabir's wall. Forty-two weeks. Solid green. And for the first time all week, I don't envy it. I can see it now for what it is: a man who never missed a day of pushing something, anything, to keep a wall green. Maybe his work is brilliant and the wall is just a side effect. Maybe the wall is the work. I don't know. I have never asked, and I am not going to ask, because the answer would tell me about him and nothing about me.

My square for today is green. One commit, the deploy, the one that mattered. Next to it, Wednesday sits grey, a hole in the wall shaped like a day I spent thinking instead of pushing. I look at it for a while. Then I close the tab, and I leave it grey, and I go home.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: NFC and RFID Feel Like Magic Because We Hid the Protocol From Users
articles.description: You tap a card. A door opens. A payment clears. Nothing visibly happens in between, and that...
articles.body_html:
You tap a card. A door opens. A payment clears. Nothing visibly happens in between, and that is exactly the point.

You have done it a thousand times. You hold your phone near a terminal, you feel the little buzz, you see the checkmark, you walk away like you just performed a minor miracle. You tap your badge to get into work. You tap your transit card to get on the train. You tap your hotel key to get into a room that, ten seconds earlier, did not know you existed.

It feels like magic because it was designed to feel like magic.

Underneath that tap is a negotiation so fast, so fussy, so paranoid about timing, that if you could hear it, it would sound less like a spell and more like two very nervous robots shouting passwords at each other in a language made of magnetic fields. The reason you do not hear it is not because it is simple. It is because an entire industry spent decades burying the complexity so you would never have to think about it.

And that burial worked a little too well.

We now live in a world where most people think NFC is just “tap to pay,” RFID is just “the thing that beeps at the store exit,” and both are basically Bluetooth but lazier. They are not. They are older, weirder, more physical, and in some ways more honest than almost any other wireless tech you use every day. NFC and RFID do not pretend distance does not matter. They embrace it. They only work when you are close, and that closeness is the security model, the user interface, and the magic trick all at once.

Let us pull the curtain back.

The tap is a handshake, not a wave

When you tap, you are not waving data through the air like Wi-Fi. You are creating a tiny, temporary power plant.

Most RFID and NFC systems work on inductive coupling. That is a fancy way of saying: one coil makes a magnetic field, another coil sits inside that field and steals just enough energy from it to wake up and talk back.

The reader is the loud one. It is constantly shouting into the void: “Anyone there? Anyone there? Anyone there?” in the form of a 13.56 MHz field for NFC and high-frequency RFID, or a lower frequency field for low-frequency tags, or a UHF field for the long-range stuff you see in warehouses.

The tag is the quiet one. Most passive tags have no battery at all. They are dead until they enter the field. Then, for a fraction of a second, they come alive. They harvest power from the reader, boot up a tiny chip, modulate that same field to send back an ID, and then go back to being a piece of plastic.

Think about how absurd that is. Your transit card is a computer with no power source that only exists when you need it. Your office badge is a zombie that wakes up when it gets close to its master. Your hotel key is a secret that only speaks when whispered to by the right lock.

NFC is the chatty cousin in this family. Where basic RFID is often one-way, a tag yelling its ID at a reader, NFC is designed for two-way conversation. Phone to terminal. Phone to phone. Phone to tag. It can read, it can write, it can emulate a card, it can do peer-to-peer. That is why your phone can both pay for coffee and read a smart poster and act like a transit card. It is playing three different roles with the same antenna, and it switches roles so fast you never notice.

The whole transaction, from field to wake to challenge to response to “approved,” happens in under half a second. Your brain interprets that speed as effortlessness. Engineers interpret it as a miracle of timing, because if either side is a millisecond late, the whole thing collapses.

We hid the protocol because the protocol is ugly

Here is the dirty secret of NFC and RFID: the user experience is clean because the protocol is not.

Underneath that tap is a stack of standards with names that sound like they were generated by a committee that hated joy: ISO 14443, ISO 15693, ISO 18092, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE DESFire, FeliCa, NTAG, ICODE. Each one has its own anti-collision rules, its own modulation scheme, its own way of saying “hey, there are two tags here, who goes first,” its own crypto, or lack of crypto, and its own hilarious legacy bugs.

MIFARE Classic, for example, is still everywhere. It is in hotel keys, transit systems, office badges, student IDs, gym memberships. It is also famously broken in ways that security researchers have been writing about since 2007. Its crypto can be cracked. Its keys can be recovered. Its sectors can be cloned if you know what you are doing and you have the right reader and you have permission to test your own cards.

And yet it persists. Why? Because it works. Because it is cheap. Because replacing every reader in every building on earth is expensive. Because “good enough for a gym locker” became “good enough for everything” and nobody wanted to be the person who told a university they had to reissue 40,000 student IDs.

This is the pattern with RFID. The protocol gets hidden not just from users, but from decision makers. A facilities manager does not buy “ISO 14443-A with MIFARE Classic 1K and a known key recovery attack.” They buy “tap badges that open doors.” A hotel chain does not buy “a system with no mutual authentication and predictable UIDs.” They buy “key cards that just work.”

The abstraction is so successful that when something goes wrong, people assume it is magic failing, not engineering failing. “My card stopped working” is rarely about magic. It is about a desynchronized counter, a damaged antenna, a reader that lost power, a tag that got demagnetized by sitting next to a magnet, or a system that was never designed to handle the edge case you just hit.

When you hide the protocol, you also hide the failure modes. And when you hide the failure modes, you create a false sense of security.

Close does not mean safe

The most seductive lie in NFC and RFID is this: because you have to be close, it must be safe.

Closeness helps. It really does. An attacker cannot sniff your NFC payment from across the street the way they could sniff an open Wi-Fi network. They have to be near you, with an antenna, at the exact moment you tap. That raises the bar.

It does not make the bar unreachable.

Proximity is not authentication. Proximity is just proximity. A tag that will talk to any reader that powers it is not verifying identity, it is just being polite. A reader that will accept any UID is not checking a credential, it is checking a serial number that can be copied.

That is why relay attacks work. That is why cloning works. That is why researchers keep demonstrating, year after year, that they can capture a tap, replay it, extend it, or trick a reader into thinking a tag is closer than it is. The attack does not break physics. It abuses trust. It says: “What if I am the reader? What if I am the tag? What if I am just a very long, very invisible wire between the two?”

Modern payment systems know this, which is why they do not just send your card number. Apple Pay and Google Pay do not send your real card number over NFC. They send a token, a one-time cryptogram, a transaction-specific blob that is useless if you steal it and try to reuse it later. That is the difference between a dumb UID and a real secure element doing real cryptography in real time.

Your office badge probably does not do that. Your hotel key probably does not do that. Your gym tag definitely does not do that. They are still playing the old game: “If you know my number, you are me.”

And the number is not secret. It is broadcast to anyone who asks nicely with a magnetic field.

This is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to understand the threat model. The question is never “is RFID secure?” The question is “secure against what, for what asset, for how long?” A $2 tag protecting a $20 locker is a different problem than a $2 tag protecting a data center. A transit card that can be cloned for a free ride is a different problem than a passport that can be skimmed in a crowd.

But when we hide the protocol, we also hide that conversation. Users assume all taps are equal. They are not. Some taps are a cryptographic handshake with a secure element. Some taps are a glorified barcode that happens to be invisible.

Why your phone made it worse, and better

Your phone ruined NFC in the best possible way.

Before smartphones, NFC was mostly a card thing. You had a card, you tapped it, done. The card did one job. It was dumb on purpose.

Then phones got NFC antennas, secure elements, host card emulation, and suddenly your phone could be ten cards at once. It could be your bank card, your transit card, your hotel key, your office badge, your loyalty card, your car key. It could also be a reader. It could read tags, write tags, clone your own tags for backup, emulate tags for testing.

That flexibility is incredible. It is also confusing, because now the same gesture, the same tap, can mean ten different protocols, ten different security levels, ten different failure modes.

You tap to pay and it fails? Is it the terminal? Is it your bank? Is it the token? Is it the antenna alignment? Is it because you have three cards in your wallet and your phone is trying to read all of them at once and getting confused by anti-collision?

You tap to open a door with your phone and it works, but your physical badge does not? Is it because the phone is emulating a different UID? Is it because the reader expects a different application identifier? Is it because the system was configured for cards, not phones, and nobody updated it?

The phone turned NFC from a single-purpose tool into a platform. Platforms are powerful. Platforms are also messy. And because the phone hides all of that mess behind a checkmark and a buzz, you never learn the difference between “NFC failed” and “the application on top of NFC failed.”

That is why troubleshooting NFC feels like voodoo. Hold it a little higher. Hold it a little lower. Take off the case. Turn it off and on again. Move it slowly. Move it fast. Sacrifice a goat. None of that is in the manual, because the manual assumes the protocol will just work. When it does not, you are left with folk magic to fix actual magic.

The real magic is not the tap, it is the agreement

Here is what actually makes NFC and RFID feel like magic: everyone agreed to pretend.

Reader makers agreed to use the same frequencies. Card makers agreed to use the same modulation. Phone makers agreed to support the same standards. Banks agreed to use tokenization. Transit agencies agreed to use the same application IDs. Hotels agreed to use the same key formats, even when those formats were insecure.

That agreement is invisible, but it is the whole trick. Without it, your phone would tap a terminal and get silence. Your badge would tap a reader and get a confused blink. Your transit card would tap a gate and get nothing.

We call it interoperability. It took decades of standards meetings, patent fights, competing formats, and at least one format war that most people never heard about. FeliCa in Japan. MIFARE in Europe. Different frequencies for different uses. Different regulations for different countries. Different power limits. Different antenna sizes.

The fact that you can land in Tokyo with an iPhone and tap your way onto a train, then land in London and tap your way onto the Tube, then land in New York and tap your way into a coffee shop, is not a natural law. It is a negotiated peace treaty between industries that usually hate each other.

And like any peace treaty, it has holes. It has legacy exceptions. It has “we will support this old broken thing because too many people still use it” clauses. It has “this system is secure enough for now” compromises.

The magic is not that the technology is perfect. The magic is that it works at all, despite being built on top of compromises that would make a security auditor cry.

So what do you do with this knowledge?

You do not need to become an RFID engineer to survive in a tap-to-everything world. But you do need to stop thinking of the tap as magic, and start thinking of it as a conversation.

First, assume every tap is a negotiation, not a blessing. If a system will accept any tag that talks to it, it is not verifying you. It is verifying that you have a thing that talks. That might be fine for a loyalty card. It is not fine for a server room.

Second, treat UID as an identifier, not a secret. Your card’s UID is like your username. It is not your password. If a system treats it like a password, that system has a design flaw, not a user flaw.

Third, respect the physical layer. NFC and RFID are physical in a way Wi-Fi is not. Antenna alignment matters. Metal matters. Interference matters. A tag stuck to a metal door will behave differently than a tag stuck to a plastic door. A phone in a thick metal case will behave differently than a phone with no case. You are not doing it wrong. You are fighting physics, and physics does not care about your user experience.

Fourth, if you are building or buying systems, ask the protocol question out loud. What standard is this? What crypto, if any? Does it do mutual authentication? Does it use rolling codes or one-time cryptograms? Can the credential be cloned, and if so, what does cloning get an attacker? How do you revoke it? Those questions sound paranoid until you are the person who has to reissue 5,000 badges because someone cloned one and posted a tutorial.

Fifth, if you are curious, test your own stuff. Legally. On your own cards, your own readers, your own systems, with permission. That is the only way the abstraction stops being scary. Read your own hotel key. See what is actually on it. Read your own transit card. See how much it reveals. Read your own office badge, if your employer allows it, and see if it is just a UID or if there is real crypto underneath.

You will be surprised how often the answer is “just a UID.” And once you see that, you will never look at a tap the same way again.

The protocol was hidden for a reason, but it does not have to stay hidden

There is a good reason we hid the protocol from users. Most people do not want to think about anti-collision algorithms while they are trying to buy coffee. They want coffee. They want the door to open. They want the train to let them through. Good design hides complexity.

Bad design hides consequences.

NFC and RFID sit exactly on that line. They hide complexity beautifully. They hide consequences terribly. They make it easy to use a credential without understanding what that credential actually proves. They make it easy to deploy a system without understanding what that system actually trusts.

The fix is not to make everyone learn ISO 14443 by heart. The fix is to make the abstraction honest. A tap that is just an ID should feel different from a tap that is a cryptographic proof. A system that can be cloned should be labeled as such. A reader that will talk to anything should not pretend it is verifying identity.

Until that happens, the magic will keep working, and the protocol will keep hiding, and most people will keep assuming that because it is fast and close and buzzes nicely, it must be safe.

It is not safe because it is close. It is useful because it is close. Those are different things.

The next time you tap, pause for half a second before you walk away. Feel the buzz. Imagine the field waking up a dead chip. Imagine the chip shouting its secrets to a reader that may or may not deserve them. Imagine the reader deciding, in milliseconds, whether to trust you.

That is not magic. That is engineering, standards, compromises, and a lot of very clever people figuring out how to make invisible conversations feel effortless.

And honestly? That is cooler than magic. Magic does not have to work twice. This does, thousands of times a day, in pockets and wallets and phones all over the world, even when we have no idea how it works.

We hid the protocol to make it feel like magic. Now that you know it is not magic, you get to use it better.

Authorized use only: your own devices, data, and systems you have permission to test.

Disclosure: I build Point Invaders with an AI coding assistant (Claude), and this article was drafted with AI help and edited by me.

Point Invaders is a neon arcade that runs in the browser: 31 missions you can play in flat 2D or full 3D, live 1v1 duels, a 20-chapter campaign, hover-car racing, and a 3D hub you fly a ship around. No download, no signup. Here's what's under the hood, and what bit me along the way.

One page, no framework, no engine

The whole arcade is four files at the top of the site: index.html, app.js, style.css and a service worker. app.js is about 8 MB of unminified, commented JavaScript — you can open it in your browser — and it's served compressed at about 2.5 MB. There's no framework and no game engine: the 3D is the game's own WebGL renderer.

Shipping one big script has a cost on a slow phone. Measured on throttled "Slow 4G" with a 4× slower CPU, first paint comes at about 3.7 s and the buttons work at about 16 s, so the page shows a "still downloading" note after six seconds rather than leaving dead buttons on screen. Splitting the script is next on my list.

2D and 3D are the same game

Every mission exists twice — a flat canvas version and a 3D one — and both score the same points onto the same boards. The 2D version runs at 60 fps on almost anything; the 3D one has LITE, NORMAL and ULTRA tiers, and LITE holds an older phone at a steady 30 fps.

Models from Unreal and Blender, in a format of my own

The ships, stations, asteroids and bosses are built in Unreal Engine and Blender, run headless from scripts, and exported into the arcade's own model format. They arrive in chunks, only the ones a screen draws, so the 2D arcade never downloads them.

Each 3D file's address carries the first eight hex digits of its SHA-256. The service worker checks a file's bytes against that stamp before keeping it, keeps good files across releases, and so an update only downloads what changed.

Drawing only what you can see

The Flight Deck was slow on laptops. Skipping the ships and stations behind the camera, no longer shading surfaces hidden behind nearer ones, and dropping a slow extra step the browser was adding to every triangle took it from about 23 fps to about 40 on the laptop I measured, with an identical picture.

iPhones and the missing colour

On iPhones the 3D models came out black or in harsh flat colours. Every browser on iOS decodes images with Safari's engine, and it threw away the colour of the textures wherever they keep extra data. The fix was to check how the browser decodes and, where colour would be lost, decode the textures in the game itself, exactly as they were made.

Every sound is code

There are no audio files. Every effect and every music loop is synthesised at runtime with Web Audio, which keeps the download small and lets a laser change pitch shot by shot. Players can write their own 16-step loop in the Drive Lab and play the arcade to it.

Live duels on a realtime database

Duels run over Firebase Realtime Database. A Pong duel streams the ball and both paddles many times a second; score races exchange scores and "hacks" that scramble the rival's board for a few seconds. When nobody answers, a labelled droid takes the seat, playing over a local stand-in for the database.

Link previews from a Worker

Chat apps never run JavaScript, so a shared challenge or level used to unfurl as the same picture. A Cloudflare Worker now answers the share paths, rewrites the page's og: tags for that challenge, level or player card, and points them at the mission's own 1200×630 image.

A bug worth knowing: centred flex columns lose their top

The sign-in screen was a flex column with justify-content: center. On a phone the column was taller than the screen, and a centred flex item that overflows overflows at both ends — the part above the top can't be scrolled to. The logo sat 32 px above the top of an iPhone 13. Auto margins (margin-block: auto on the child) centre when there's room and fall to zero when there isn't.

Releasing without breaking returning players

A release is a number written in six places (the service worker's cache name and shell, the two ?v= stamps in the page, and the newest "What's new" entry). A check script verifies they agree, that every asset stamp matches its file, and that nothing unreferenced is published; a Playwright smoke test then boots the real page against the Firebase emulators.

Working with an AI coding assistant

Most of the code is written by Claude from my direction, release by release: I decide what the next version should do and how it should feel, test it, and send it back until it's right. The tests and the check script matter more for that, not less.

You can play it at https://pointinvaders.com. I'd like to hear where you got stuck in the first minute, and how 3D runs on your machine.

articles.title: Building a listening-practice video player: the design decisions that mattered
articles.description: I'm the developer of Earu, a desktop video player for practicing listening in a second language. It...
articles.body_html:
I'm the developer of Earu, a desktop video player for practicing listening in a second language. It started as a practice tool for my own kids and is meant for anyone learning a second language. This post is mostly about the engineering and design choices behind it: how subtitles get covered, how they get re-timed against the audio, how the exercises are generated and graded, and what I threw away. The product part is short and sits at the end.

Where it came from

I started by helping my kids practice listening with videos they already liked, no textbook: loop one line, put the heard words back in order, read along and get checked, re-test missed words a few days later. The numbers in the app were tuned during those sessions.

The idea is simple. Listening and speaking are the fastest route to a second language, and without enough input you can't produce anything. Many learners can read subtitles fine and still can't hear the sentence. So the player makes you listen first and turns whatever you were going to watch anyway into practice. There is no fixed curriculum: Earu runs on your own interests, and only decides what to ask you about the video you picked.

The name comes from a Chinese idiom about learning by soaking in something every day. "Earu" is a rough phonetic match.

Covering subtitles instead of hiding them

The first design flip: subtitles in the language you're learning are covered by default, and your native-language subtitles are not. Each subtitle layer has three states: shown, hidden, covered.

"Covered" is deliberately not "hidden". A covered subtitle is still there, blurred into a soft fog that keeps the original width and line count so the layout doesn't jump. Move the mouse across it and the fog parts under the cursor; stop, and after about a third of a second it drifts back over a few seconds. You glance when you're lost and return to listening, with no trip to settings.

During an exercise the learning-language subtitle is always covered and hovering doesn't reveal it; a deliberate peek is a click and counts as a hint. Annotations like [music] are never covered.

The implementation went through two versions, and the second is the interesting one. Each covered element is two stacked layers: the blurred text, and a crisp clone of the same text behind it. Every "gust" of the mouse is a soft-edged hole. The blurred layer's mask is "everything minus the gusts", and the clone's mask is "only the gusts".

My first version drew each gust as its own radial gradient. A fast swipe produced over a hundred gradient layers per element, each repainted at full size every frame. The fix was to composite all gusts into one tiny alpha bitmap per frame and use it as the mask, stretched over the element:

every frame:
  alpha = small grid, size ~ element / (0.16 * font height)
  for gust in gusts: stamp soft circle into alpha
  blurredLayer.mask = everything minus alpha
  cloneLayer.mask   = alpha

Because the grid scales with font size, cost per gust stays roughly constant. WebKit engines load mask images asynchronously, so swapping one every frame made the line flicker out; there the next mask is decoded off-screen first. Where small masks aren't supported, it falls back to gradients.

Re-timing subtitles against the audio

Subtitles one or two seconds off are miserable for listening practice, and plenty of files are. So the player checks the audio itself.

A small voice-activity model runs in a Web Worker on 32 ms blocks of 16 kHz mono audio and outputs a "someone is speaking" probability for each block. The subtitle cues are also a speech/no-speech signal. The job is to find the straight line real_time = k * subtitle_time + b that makes the two signals line up best.

Some choices that made it reliable: the scale factor only tries values near common frame-rate mismatches (1, 23.976 vs 24, 23.976 vs 25 and inverses), because free search finds nonsense; the offset is searched within about 10 seconds, coarse then fine; and the result must agree with itself. The video is cut into up to five segments, and each segment's own best offset must sit within a quarter of a second of the global line, otherwise the answer is thrown away. Under ten minutes only the offset is fitted, since short clips produced fake scale values, and corrections smaller than roughly 0.15 to 0.2 seconds are ignored.

In my tests on two real episodes, correct subtitles correlated with the audio at about 0.5 and subtitles from the wrong episode below 0.1; the thresholds are built on that gap. When confident, the player applies the corrected timing and shows a small icon with the maximum shift in seconds. Click it and you get the original timing back, because an automatic fix you can't undo is a bug waiting to happen.

Sort: pre-placing blocks so nobody gets stuck

Sort splits the sentence you just heard into shuffled word blocks, and you put them back in order while it loops. Nobody can reliably hear every function word in a 20-word sentence, so long ones start with some blocks placed and locked, more at lower difficulty levels. On the default level, up to eight words get none, then one more per two extra words.

Which blocks get placed matters more than how many. In order of preference: the first and last word (anchors); names (audible but unguessable spelling); words rarer than your difficulty level, rarest first (needs a word-frequency table, so only for languages that have one); then whatever is left, spread evenly by always picking the word farthest from those already chosen.

The same sentence at the same level always gets the same pre-placed words, including after "shuffle again"; otherwise redoing a question would hand you a different question. The shuffle is a plain Fisher-Yates plus one rule: if it lands on the correct order, swap the first two blocks, so a two-word sentence always arrives reversed.

Correctness is checked by text per position, not by block identity, so with two "the" in a sentence either can go in either slot. Sort and Dictation share the pre-placement code: I noticed the same sentence showed different fixed words in the two exercises, which felt wrong, so now there's one function both ask.

Dictation: strict spelling, lenient formatting

Dictation is one box per word. You type, press Enter, and everything is judged at once: correct boxes lock, wrong ones turn red.

Spelling is strict. Everything that isn't spelling is forgiven:

  • Case doesn't matter.
  • Straight and curly apostrophes are the same character.
  • Numbers match in either form. A run of adjacent number words like "twenty five" or "one hundred and five" collapses into a single box that accepts both "25" and the spelled-out version. It doesn't merge "one two three", because that's counting, not a number. A lone "hundred" isn't treated as a number either.
  • Spanish has its own rules: 1.000 equals 1000, a missing accent is accepted but marked yellow with the right spelling, and a wrong accent or missing ñ is an error.

The boxes come from the same tokenizer used for Sort and scoring, so the box count can never exceed the word count the scoring side uses.

Read-aloud: score per word, and a pass mark the UI doesn't know

For Read-aloud you listen to the original line, then read it into the microphone, and what you said is compared word by word with the original. Words come back green or red. The score is the share of scored words you got right, rounded down.

Not every word is scored: names and a short list of throwaway words are skipped, since a recognizer is often wrong on exactly those. The pass mark defaults to 85 and can be moved between 70 and 100.

The page does not know the pass mark. The UI never computes "did they pass"; it draws the verdict and per-word results it receives, stars included, so the screen and the scoring can't drift apart. Miss the same sentence five times in a row and the app offers another one. Silent or near-silent recordings don't count as an attempt.

Don't let people farm points

Points exist so a day's practice means something. Each sentence has a difficulty from L0 to L5. L0 sentences have no real content: interjections, forms of address, names, one-or-two-word lines. You can practice them, but a correct answer scores zero, otherwise "Oh" and "Hey" would be a points machine.

I made L0 a plain rule set rather than asking AI "does this line have content?". Asked twice, the AI disagreed with itself, which makes it a bad judge for anything that touches scoring. Other limits: the same sentence scores once per 15 days across Sort and Dictation, very fast answers don't count, and short sentences are capped per day.

Translating once for everyone

Native-language subtitles come from AI translation, not from the video, so without care every user opening a popular video would repeat the same work. Translation is keyed by a fingerprint: SHA-256 over the normalized subtitle lines. The client asks whether a translation exists, uses it if so, and otherwise uploads the subtitle text (never the video) and polls.

The fingerprint is versioned by the sentence-merging rules: when I improved how raw cues merge into sentences, every fingerprint would have changed, so the previous fingerprint can be computed too and unchanged sentences carry their translations over. Files on cloud drives and home media libraries get a cheap file fingerprint instead: a hash of the file size plus the first 64 KB.

One table of feature names, fourteen interface languages

Earu has twelve languages you can learn and fourteen interface languages (Simplified and Traditional Chinese counted separately). Feature names like Sort, Dictation, Read-aloud, Daily Quiz, Word notebook, Cover, Study plan, Hint and Sentence breakdown appear in a great many strings.

Renaming one used to mean a search through every locale file. So there's now a single table, one row per language, and every other string refers to a name with a token:

"Opens when today's {@sort} reaches {t} points"

Locale files are wrapped in a loader that substitutes the tokens when it loads. Everything downstream, including the lookup code and the tests, sees a normal finished sentence. A lint script fails the build if a locale file spells a feature name out directly, with a short allow-list for words that merely look the same.

Languages with case or articles (German, French, Russian and others) carry extra forms per name, such as a lowercase form or a past participle for "covered". Renaming a feature is a one-row edit. Static pages like the privacy policy can't use tokens, so a snapshot test flags which ones to update.

Why it's a desktop app, and how it ships

The first prototype lived in a browser tab. Then I wanted to play videos from a NAS at home and hit two walls: the page is HTTPS while most NAS endpoints are plain HTTP, so browsers block it as mixed content, and the NAS sends no cross-origin permissions, a second block behind the first. So Earu is a desktop app, for Windows and macOS.

The architecture is thin on purpose. The desktop shell is an Electron window that loads the Earu website and injects a small bridge object into the page. The bridge exposes the few things only a native shell can do. The page is otherwise a normal web app that treats the bridge as optional: if a method isn't there, the feature counts as unavailable rather than crashing the screen. The rules that differ between store builds and direct downloads all hang off one "which build is this" field instead of being scattered through components.

The practical effect is that interface changes ship as a normal web deploy, and users don't have to reinstall for them.

What I gave up

A fixed curriculum. Ordering lessons from easy to hard looks systematic, and I understand why people want that. But you can only keep going with videos you're happy to rewatch. Earu has no curriculum, and your own interests decide what you study. The Study plan sets how much you do per day, not what you learn. It's a workload, not a course.

CEFR levels for the built-in library. In my first try a picture book came out as C1 and a video at 200 words per minute as A2, the opposite of how they sound. I replaced it with three coarse levels based mostly on speech rate, tuned against blind ratings.

Letting AI fill the gaps. If a word isn't in the dictionary, the word card says so. It doesn't ask AI to invent a definition. I would rather have a missing entry than a wrong one that ends up in someone's notebook.

Using it

Earu plays videos from a built-in library, your computer, cloud drives and a home media server; files on your computer stay there. English is the most complete language, and twelve are supported in total.

I'm the developer, and I'd like to hear how it works for you, especially where it feels off.

  • Windows: Microsoft Store, or from earu.ai
  • macOS: from earu.ai

articles.title: I made my app's 2-minute launch film entirely in code
articles.description: My app, Orbit OS, needed a film: two minutes that show every feature of a TV home screen and walk...
articles.body_html:
My app, Orbit OS, needed a film: two minutes that show every feature of a TV home screen and walk through the whole setup. I don't use editing software, so my AI pair programmer and I wrote the film instead.

Here's how it works, and why I'd do it this way again.

Every frame is a function of time

The film is one HTML page. It has the TV, the phone, the captions and the setup guide as plain DOM, and one function:

function seek(t) { apply(compute(t), t); }

compute(t) builds a state object for the time t: where the TV sits, which screen layer is visible, where the home row's focus is, which phone screenshot is showing, how far each caption has risen. apply() writes that state onto the DOM. Nothing animates by itself: there are no CSS transitions and no requestAnimationFrame. The same t always gives the same frame.

That one rule makes everything else easy. A scene is just a time range:

if (t >= 31.2 && t < 40.8) { // Live TV
  S.L.live = t >= 31.75 ? 1 : 0;
  S.live.open = E.out5(lin(t, 31.75, 32.3));   // the card opens into the picture
  S.live.guide = win(t, 33.0, 36.5, 0.35, 0.35); // the guide slides in, then out
  if (t >= 35.4) { S.live.ch = [19, 'Aastha']; S.live.zap = t - 35.4; }
}

The "launcher" in the film is the real one's design rebuilt in DOM: a row of cards on the inside of a cylinder (translate3d plus rotateY from the card's distance to the focus), a glow that takes the focused app's colour, and a streak of light across the focused card. The phone screens are real screenshots of the app, captured with Playwright from its own demo mode.

Rendering: Playwright as a frame grabber 

for (let f = first; f <= last; f++) {
  await page.evaluate((t) => window.seek(t), f / FPS);
  await page.screenshot({ path: `frames/f${String(f).padStart(5, '0')}.jpg`, type: 'jpeg', quality: 95 });
}

Six pages render in parallel. At 1080p and 30 fps the 4,050 frames take about 45 seconds on a laptop. With deviceScaleFactor: 2 the same page renders at 4K, and at 60 fps that's 8,100 frames for the final version. ffmpeg joins them with the sound.

One gotcha: anything random has to be random per frame, not per call, or a re-render changes the picture. The TV static uses a hash of the time instead of Math.random().

The music is code too

No stock music and no samples: score.py writes the soundtrack with numpy, on the same cue list as the picture. Plucked notes are Karplus-Strong strings. The bells use FM synthesis. Pads are detuned saws through a spectral low-pass. Every UI click in the film has a tick at the same timestamp. A noise-burst reverb glues it together, a sidechain makes the pad breathe with the kick, and a two-pass loudnorm brings it to -14 LUFS for YouTube and X.

def pluck(f, dur=0.5, level=0.18):
    P = int(SR / f)                      # one period of the string
    out = np.zeros(int(dur * SR) + P)
    out[:P] = rng.uniform(-1, 1, P)      # pluck: a burst of noise
    for i in range(P, len(out) - P, P):  # each period is the last one, averaged and damped
        prev = out[i - P:i]
        shifted = np.concatenate(([out[i - P - 1]], prev[:-1]))
        out[i:i + P] = 0.997 * 0.5 * (prev + shifted)
    ...

Why bother

  • Fixes are one line. "The phone covers the toast in step 3" became left: 510px, then a 45-second re-render.
  • The film can't drift from the app. The screens are the app's own, and the captions sit in an array next to their times.
  • It's reviewable. Every scene was checked by rendering stills at chosen times and looking at contact sheets, the same way you'd review a UI.

The source for Orbit OS is GPL-3.0 on GitHub, and the app is free on Google Play. If you've rendered video from code another way, I'd love to hear how.

Written with my AI assistant, from the film's real code.

articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge  My pulse climbed most when a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

My pulse climbed most when a practice tower cleared me to land. The take-off clearance was not far behind.

I was at my desk with a headset on, talking to a simulated tower while the camera followed my pulse. Nothing was moving. Still, it was as if I could really see myself taking off, and then landing.

Both are short messages. The taxi clearance at the start is much longer: a runway, a QNH, a holding point and a route, to read back in order. In that session, my pulse didn't follow the length of the message. It followed what the words meant.

In October I built a practice tower for a friend who is shy about speaking English on the radio. It talks, it listens, and it says "negative" when the QNH is wrong. This month I pointed a camera at the person talking to it.

What I Built

Readback is a radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, and you read back out loud. Meanwhile, the camera follows your pulse and your breathing with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK.

Talking to the tower is one of the things that scare people when they learn to fly. You know the phraseology at home. Then a controller reads you a clearance in one breath, and you have to say it back, in order, while the frequency waits.

A session goes like this:

  1. A consent screen comes first. It says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage, and how to stop.
  2. A calm minute. You sit the way you will for the radio and breathe normally. That minute becomes your reference, for this session only.
  3. A circuit at Isola, a made-up aerodrome: taxi, take-off, a touch and go, a full stop. You hold the space bar to talk. The runway, the QNH and the wind change every game, and a wrong readback gets "negative".
  4. On the side, your pulse and your breathing, shown as differences from your calm minute.
  5. A breathing guide, if your breathing picked up while you listened. It offers three slow breaths before your readback. The tower waits.
  6. A timeline after the circuit. It puts first the messages after which your pulse climbed most.

It's a mirror for practice, not a measure of health. It compares you with yourself, and with nothing else. Like the October tower, it's a game, not an approved training device: your instructor and your country's phraseology manual are the reference.

Demo

The video shows the consent screen, the calm minute, an exchange with the tower, the breathing guide and the timeline. The camera preview is blurred.

Code

dsiacci / readback

Readback

A radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, you read back out loud, and the camera follows your pulse and your breathing while you do, with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. Before your readback, if your breathing has picked up while you listened, a short breathing guide offers itself: the tower can wait. After the circuit, a timeline shows which messages made your pulse climb, next to what the tower said and what you read back.

A mirror for practice, not a measure of health. Readback compares you only with yourself, with a calm minute taken at the start of each session. It makes no medical claim, shows no normal or abnormal value, and never says whether anyone is fit to fly. It is a practice game, not an approved training device: your flight instructor and your country's official phraseology manual are…

View on GitHub

Electron and plain JavaScript, under the Apache 2.0 licence. On a Mac with Apple Silicon: npm install, then npm run setup:tower once, your Presage key in ~/.config/readback/presage.key, and npm start. No camera at hand? The first screen offers simulated signals, labelled as such everywhere.

The tower is my October project, phraseology. Readback runs it unchanged, as a separate program on the same computer. Everything that reacts to the camera is new.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Readback asks the SDK for three signals, and nothing else:

Signal What the SDK gives What Readback does with it
Pulse rate an average over 12 seconds your reference, the live difference, and the climb after each message
Breathing rate an average over 30 seconds your reference during the calm minute
Chest movement the breathing waveform breaths counted while you listen, and the breathing guide

The wiring is the SDK's renderer entry point, with telemetry off:

const sdk = new SmartSpectraSDK({
  apiKey,  // read by the main process from a file in your home folder
  requestedMetrics: [MetricType.CHEST_BREATHING, MetricType.BREATHING_RATE, MetricType.PULSE_RATE],
  enableTelemetry: false,
});
sdk.on('metrics', (buf) => store.add(decodeMetrics(buf)));
sdk.on('validationStatus', (code) => showHint(code)); // "face the camera", "more light"…
await sdk.start(); // only after the consent screen

The most useful page was Presage's model card. It says the breathing rate doesn't hold while the person is talking. But a radio exchange is talking, a few seconds of listening, and talking again. There are never 30 quiet seconds.

So I used the chest movement instead, which the SDK streams next to the rate. Readback takes the moments when you are listening, removes the slow drift, and counts the breaths. The same count on the calm minute gives the reference. It's a rough count, but it's enough to notice that you breathe faster than at rest. Readback never shows a breathing number while you talk.

When that count is up by 4 breaths a minute or more, the breathing guide opens. You can change that threshold, or turn the guide off. It breathes four seconds in and six out, three times, and draws your own chest moving under the circle. The space bar skips it.

The timeline needed one correction. My first version ranked the messages by how high the pulse went above the calm minute. On the first test, with simulated signals, every message after a "negative" looked stressful, because the pulse was still up. Now a message's climb starts from the pulse at its first word. The level against the calm minute sits next to it.

Here is the timeline after my own circuit:

The clearance to land came first, with a climb of 14 beats per minute. The take-off clearance came third. Between them, the tower's request to read back the vacate instruction, which came right after landing, while my pulse was still up. Before both clearances, the breathing guide opened, and both times I skipped it to read back.

HRV and facial expressions are left out on purpose. HRV needs a full minute, longer than an exchange. And a label like "fear" on someone learning would be a judgement, with nothing true to add to the practice.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. Radio nerves are part of learning to fly, and the usual advice is "practise more", with nobody to practise with. Readback gives you a tower to practise with, and a mirror of what it does to you. The design follows from consent and from the SDK's limits: the camera opens only after you agree, the preview is blurred by default, the numbers are differences from your own calm minute, breathing is read only while you listen, and nothing is saved unless you ask.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The signal changes the conversation, not just a dashboard. When your breathing has picked up, the tower waits for you, and you watch your own chest move under the breathing circle. The tower's voice goes through a small radio filter with a squelch, and the screens use B612, the typeface designed for cockpit displays.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent first. The first screen says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage and how to stop. The camera opens only after "I agree, turn the camera on". The microphone is a separate choice; without it, you type your readbacks. Until you agree, the app refuses every camera and microphone request.
  • Visible and stoppable. "Camera on" and "Stop camera" stay at the top while the camera runs. Closing the window stops everything, and the camera turns off at the end of each circuit.
  • Images: never recorded, saved or sent by Readback.
  • Your voice: kept in memory while you hold the key, transcribed on the same computer by the tower, then dropped. Never written to disk.
  • Measurements: in memory during the session. Saved only if you press "Save on this computer", as a small file with your reference, the tower's messages, whether each readback was accepted, and the climbs. No image, no audio, no transcript. One button deletes every saved session.
  • What goes to Presage: the SDK computes pulse and breathing on the computer. It contacts Presage's service to check the API key and the plan. The SDK's usage telemetry is on by default; Readback turns it off.
  • No AI service. No language model writes anything about you. The tower's readback checks are plain rules.
  • Nothing else leaves the computer. The app's page can't reach the network. Setup downloads the packages and the speech models once; after that, the tower runs offline.

I built Readback to practise the long readbacks. My pulse cared about two short sentences.

Pilots: which radio call still gets you, years after the licence?

articles.title: How I Built an Undertale-Inspired Bad Time Simulator in Pure JavaScript (60 FPS on Browser)
articles.description: Every indie developer has that one passion project inspired by a game they love. For me, that...
articles.body_html:
Every indie developer has that one passion project inspired by a game they love. For me, that obsession was the notorious Sans genocide boss fight from Undertale.

If you've ever played it, you know the feeling: hours of muscle memory wiped out in seconds by a barrage of frame-perfect bones, spinning platforms, and laser-firing Gaster Blasters. The problem? If you want to practice specific attack patterns, you traditionally have to replay the entire game or mess around with local desktop save files.

I asked myself: Could I rebuild a pixel-perfect, deterministic bullet-hell engine right inside the web browser that runs at a locked 60 FPS without any downloads?

That idea led to the creation of Bad Time Simulator.

Here is the technical retrospective of how I engineered the engine, handled sub-pixel collision physics, optimized high-volume particle pooling, and brought retro bullet-hell mechanics to the modern web.

The Core Goals

Before writing a single line of code, I set three non-negotiable architectural requirements:

  1. Zero Input Latency: When dodging bullet hell, even a 16ms frame drop feels catastrophic.
  2. Sub-Pixel Deterministic Hitboxes: Replicating the distinct Red Soul (free directional flight) vs. Blue Soul (gravity-affected platformer physics) precision.
  3. Instant Accessibility: Lightweight, fully responsive across both desktop (keyboard) and mobile touchscreens.

The Tech Stack

I deliberately chose a lightweight, dependency-free architecture:

  • Rendering Layer: HTML5 Canvas 2D Context with offscreen double buffering (bypassing heavy third-party engine overhead).
  • Core Engine: Vanilla TypeScript/JavaScript using an explicit fixed-step requestAnimationFrame game loop.
  • Audio Engine: Web Audio API for zero-delay retro SFX playback and chiptune sound wave synchronization.
  • State & Attack Sequencing: Finite State Machine (FSM) defining procedural attack phases and bullet timing scripts.

Engineering Challenges & Solutions

1. Object Pooling for 200+ Active Projectiles

In the most frantic phases of the battle, the screen is flooded with moving bones, lasers, and particle debris. Allocating and destroying JavaScript objects inside the render loop causes frequent Garbage Collection (GC) pauses, resulting in micro-stutters.

To eliminate GC hitches, I implemented an Entity Object Pool:

class BonePool {
  constructor(initialSize = 300) {
    this.pool = Array.from({ length: initialSize }, () => new Bone());
    this.activeBones = [];
  }

  spawn(x, y, height, speedX, type = 'white') {
    const bone = this.pool.pop() || new Bone();
    bone.init(x, y, height, speedX, type);
    this.activeBones.push(bone);
    return bone;
  }

  recycle(bone) {
    const index = this.activeBones.indexOf(bone);
    if (index !== -1) {
      this.activeBones.splice(index, 1);
      bone.reset();
      this.pool.push(bone);
    }
  }
}

By reusing instantiated nodes, runtime heap allocation dropped to near-zero during combat loops, maintaining a solid 60 FPS on low-power mobile browsers.

2. The Dual-Soul Physics Engine

Recreating the two distinct movement states of the player soul required different physics models:

  • Red Soul (Omnidirectional Mode): Fixed velocity vector with instantaneous acceleration and deceleration.
  • Blue Soul (Gravity Mode): Standard jump-curve trajectory with gravity constants ($g$), terminal velocity caps, and AABB platform collision snapping. 
updateSoulPhysics(deltaTime) {
  if (this.mode === 'RED') {
    this.x += this.inputVector.x * this.speed * deltaTime;
    this.y += this.inputVector.y * this.speed * deltaTime;
  } else if (this.mode === 'BLUE') {
    // Apply gravity
    this.velocityY = Math.min(this.velocityY + this.gravity * deltaTime, this.terminalVelocity);
    this.y += this.velocityY * deltaTime;
    this.x += this.inputVector.x * this.horizontalSpeed * deltaTime;

    // Platform snapping check
    this.resolvePlatformCollisions();
  }
  this.clampToBounds(this.battleBox);
}

3. Audio & Beam Synchronization (The Gaster Blaster)

One of the most satisfying visual cues is the Gaster Blaster: it spawns, rotates toward the player, charges for a fixed duration, and beams down a wide column of damage.

To sync the visual beam expansion with the Web Audio sound explosion:

  • Audio samples are pre-decoded into memory buffers via AudioContext.decodeAudioData.
  • Sound trigger timestamps are locked to the FSM attack timeline rather than asynchronous DOM callbacks, guaranteeing audio-visual alignment down to the millisecond.

Live Demo & Try It Out

You can play, test your dodging skills, and practice attack patterns directly in your browser without any installation:

Try the Bad Time Simulator Here

Whether you want to warm up your reflexes or analyze how classic 2D retro bosses were constructed, give it a spin!

Lessons Learned & What's Next

Building this project reinforced a few key web game development truths:

  1. Canvas 2D is still remarkably fast: You don't always need complex WebGL shaders for retro 2D games; clean object lifecycle management and efficient math often provide better performance dividends.
  2. Deterministic timing is everything: Avoid tying game physics directly to fluctuating refresh rates (like 120Hz vs 60Hz displays). Always use a fixed-delta timestep loop.

Future roadmap:

  • [ ] Attack Pattern Editor: allowing players to design custom bullet-hell choreography via JSON.
  • [ ] Global Leaderboards for endless survival mode.
  • [ ] Gamepad / Controller API integration.

Have you ever rebuilt a retro game mechanic on the modern web? Let me know your thoughts or feedback in the comments below!

articles.title: Three date bugs in a 10-line age calculator (and the TZ= trick that exposes them)
articles.description: Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the...
articles.body_html:
Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the days, borrow when something goes negative. Mine had all of that. It still told a user born on 31 January that on 1 March they were 26 years, 1 month and −2 days old. On their birthday it said their next birthday was 365 days away.

Here are the three bugs and how I fixed them. If you've ever written new Date(input.value), at least one of them is probably in your code too.

Bug 1: new Date("2026-05-15") is not 15 May in your time zone

An <input type="date"> gives you a string like "2026-05-15". Passing that to new Date() creates midnight UTC, not local midnight. That's ECMAScript's rule for date-only ISO strings.

Then the code calls getDate(), getMonth() and so on, which read local time. In Pakistan (UTC+5) that UTC midnight is 05:00 on the same day, so the date looks right. But:

const nb = new Date(b.getFullYear(), a.getMonth(), a.getDate()); // local midnight
if (nb < b) nb.setFullYear(b.getFullYear() + 1);

On the birthday, nb is 00:00 local and b is 05:00 local, so nb < b is true and the next birthday jumps a year ahead. Hence "365 days".

In US time zones it's worse. UTC midnight is still the previous day locally, so every result was off by a day. The same inputs gave "1 month −2 days" in Lahore and "0 months 29 days" in Los Angeles.

Fix: parse the string yourself as a local calendar date.

function pd(v) {
  const [y, m, d] = v.split('-').map(Number);
  return new Date(y, m - 1, d);       // local midnight
}

The same trap applies the other way. input.valueAsDate = new Date() sets the field to today in UTC, which shows yesterday's date for anyone ahead of UTC just after midnight. Build the YYYY-MM-DD string from the local getFullYear/getMonth/getDate instead.

Bug 2: borrowing days from the wrong month

The classic algorithm:

let d = b.getDate() - a.getDate();
if (d < 0) {
  mo--;
  d += new Date(b.getFullYear(), b.getMonth(), 0).getDate(); // days in previous month
}

Born 31 Jan, today is 1 March: d = 1 - 31 = -30. Borrow February's 28 days and you get −2. The borrow assumes the previous month is long enough to absorb the difference, and February isn't.

Bug 3: there's no single "right" way to borrow, so define one

What is 31 January + 1 month? There's no 31 February. You have to choose, and the common choice (it's what most date libraries do) is to clamp to the last day of the month: 31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb, or 29 in a leap year.

Once you've chosen, the cleanest algorithm doesn't borrow at all. Count whole months, then count the leftover days:

function addMonths(t, n) {
  const y = t.getFullYear(), m = t.getMonth() + n;
  const last = new Date(y, m + 1, 0).getDate();          // last day of target month
  return new Date(y, m, Math.min(t.getDate(), last));     // clamp
}
function dayDiff(x, y) {                                   // DST-safe
  return Math.round((Date.UTC(y.getFullYear(), y.getMonth(), y.getDate())
                   - Date.UTC(x.getFullYear(), x.getMonth(), x.getDate())) / 864e5);
}
function age(a, b) {
  let months = (b.getFullYear() - a.getFullYear()) * 12 + (b.getMonth() - a.getMonth());
  if (addMonths(a, months) > b) months--;                  // this month's anniversary not reached
  const days = dayDiff(addMonths(a, months), b);
  return { years: Math.floor(months / 12), months: months % 12, days };
}

Days can never be negative now, because they're measured forward from the last whole-month anniversary. 31 Jan → 1 Mar is 1 month (to 28 Feb) plus 1 day.

The next birthday falls out of the same helper: addMonths(dob, 12 * yearsSince). That also handles 29 February birthdays (celebrated on the 28th in non-leap years).

How I tested it

  • Edge cases: month ends, 29 Feb in leap and non-leap years, the birthday itself, 31 Dec → 1 Jan.
  • Three time zones: each case ran under TZ=Asia/Karachi, TZ=America/Los_Angeles and TZ=UTC in Node. All three now print identical results. The old code gave a different answer in each zone I tried.
  • 20,000 random date pairs: asserting that days are never negative and months stay within 0–11.

The TZ= trick is the takeaway. If your date code gives different answers when you change the time zone of the machine running it, you have a bug, even if it looks fine where you live.

The calculator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. People mostly use it to check job and admission age limits "as on" a closing date, where being one day off actually matters.

articles.title: I backtested "important questions" on 23 real exam papers. Topic prediction barely beat random.
articles.description: Every exam season, students at my university (AKTU, a state technical university in India with lakhs...
articles.body_html:
Every exam season, students at my university (AKTU, a state technical university in India with lakhs of engineering students) share "important questions" lists. Telegram channels, YouTube, coaching PDFs. Everyone claims their list covers "80% of the paper".

I run Ryzenstudy, a free archive of about 1,600 AKTU previous year papers. Since I already had the papers as OCR text, I wanted to know: does any of this actually work? So I built the obvious predictor and tested it the honest way, on papers it had never seen.

The setup

  • Data: OCR'd question text from AKTU end-semester papers, sessions 2021-22 to 2025-26.
  • Unit of analysis: every question row with its marks (Section A short, Section B medium, Section C long).
  • Labels: each question tagged with a syllabus topic and a "question family" (same question, reworded).
  • Predictor: rank topics by how often they appeared in earlier papers, call the top ones Tier 1 and Tier 2. This is basically what every "important questions" list does.
  • Test: blind backtest. For each of 10 B.Tech subjects, hide one paper, build tiers from the older papers only, then measure how many of the hidden paper's marks fall inside the predicted tiers. 23 held-out papers in total.
  • Baseline: a random set of topics of the same size. If the predictor can't beat that clearly, it isn't predicting anything.

The results

What I measured Result
Marks covered by Tier 1 + Tier 2 topics 61%
Marks covered by a random topic set of the same size 51%
Gain from weighting recent papers more < 1 point
Hidden-paper questions that matched an earlier question family 26%
Marks in a new paper that repeat an earlier question ~43%

Topic prediction gets you +10 points over random. That's it. A syllabus is small enough that any reasonable set of topics covers half the paper by accident, so "covers 60% of the paper" sounds impressive and means very little.

Recency weighting, the thing every "this year's expected questions" video leans on, did nothing measurable.

What actually holds up: repeats

The one number that survived is boring and useful: about 43% of a new paper's marks are questions that already appeared in an earlier paper (reworded, but the same question). For some subjects it's much higher. Electromagnetic Field Theory was 54%, Constitution of India 59%.

That's not prediction, it's just a fact about how papers get set. So I stopped calling anything "important" and built a repeat bank instead: every question that has appeared more than once, grouped by family, with the years it appeared.

You can see them here: AKTU important questions (repeat bank). Each subject page shows its own honest numbers, including the weak ones. Web Technology repeats only about 10%, and the page says so.

Things that broke along the way

  • OCR merges rows. Section A sub-questions (h), (i), (j) often came out as one line. I had to split them, or the marks totals went wrong.
  • Universities reuse subject codes. At AKTU, KCS502 was Compiler Design but BCS502 is Web Technology. Matching papers by code alone silently mixed two subjects, so I now match on code and title.
  • Partial papers poison the stats. A scan missing Section C makes a subject look like it has no long questions. Papers with fewer than 15 question rows are now excluded.
  • Maths is hard to OCR. For Engineering Mathematics, over 40% of the top questions came out as garbage, so those pages are held back instead of published with bad data.

Takeaways

  1. If someone sells "80% guaranteed" important questions, ask what their random baseline is.
  2. Solve previous year papers first, not prediction lists. Repeats are the only effect big enough to matter. All the papers I used are free here: AKTU previous year question papers.
  3. Backtest anything that claims to predict. It took me one evening to write the test, and it changed what I built.

If you've done something similar for your university's papers, I'd like to compare numbers.

articles.title: I built a CLI that turns any place on Earth into a pixel-art diorama
articles.description: Type a place, get an isometric pixel-art poster, video or GIF built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps data.
articles.body_html:
I wanted a picture of the street I grew up on, drawn like an old isometric game. I couldn't find a tool that did it from real map data, so I wrote one.

npx dioramap "Eiffel Tower, Paris" -t night

About ten seconds later there's a poster in the current folder. A place name, a street address or a pair of coordinates all work.

Where the data comes from

  • Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's geocoder, finds the place.
  • Roads, water, parks and land use come from OpenFreeMap vector tiles.
  • Buildings come from Overture Maps, which merges OpenStreetMap with Microsoft and Google footprints. Towns that are thin on OpenStreetMap still get their buildings this way.

The buildings are read straight out of Overture's PMTiles file and the rest from static vector tiles. There's no server of mine in the middle, so there's no API key and no rate limit.

Heights and roofs

Buildings keep their mapped parts, heights and roof shapes. That's how the Eiffel Tower gets its tapering legs and St Peter's gets its dome. When nobody mapped a height, I guess one from the footprint and how built-up the area around it is.

Making it look like pixel art

three.js renders the scene into a render target at a third of the final size, using the 2:1 camera angle pixel artists use. On top of that go outlines, sun shadows, lit windows, trees and cars. Then the image is scaled up with nearest-neighbour filtering, so every edge stays hard.

There's no AI model anywhere in the pipeline. That's why it never comes out blurry.

Video and GIF

--video makes an MP4 where the flat street map rises into the city building by building, then night falls and the lights come on. The headless browser encodes the H.264 frames with WebCodecs and I write the MP4 container myself, so you don't need ffmpeg.

npx dioramap "Dubai Marina" -t night --video
npx dioramap "Rialto Bridge, Venice" --gif

What it can't do

How good it looks depends on the map data. Big cities come out great. A village nobody has mapped in detail looks sparse, and dioramap won't invent buildings to fill it in.

Try it

You need Node 20 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium installed.

npx dioramap "your street, your city"

The code is MIT licensed: https://github.com/omlahore/dioramap

If you render your hometown, I'd like to see it.
